pian01.summary: Book 1, 'Xue er' (Learning), is about study, filial and brotherly duty, conscientiousness and trustworthiness, and caution. It opens by setting out the cultivation of the noble person (junzi): love of learning, loyalty in doing things for others, good faith with friends, filial piety as the root of humaneness, and harmony as the value of ritual.
pian01.translation:
The Master said: "To learn something and then practise it at the right time - is that not a pleasure? To have friends come from far away - is that not a joy? To go unrecognised by others and feel no resentment - is that not the mark of a noble person (junzi)?"
Master You said: "There are few people who are good sons and good younger brothers and yet like to defy their superiors. And there has never been one who does not like to defy his superiors but likes to stir up rebellion. The noble person works at the root; when the root is established, the Way grows from it. Being a good son and a good younger brother - is that not the root of humaneness (ren)?"
The Master said: "Clever words and an ingratiating look - there is little humaneness in them."
Master Zeng said: "Every day I examine myself on three counts. In doing things for others, have I been less than loyal? In dealing with friends, have I been less than trustworthy? Have I failed to practise what was handed down to me?"
The Master said: "To lead a state of a thousand chariots, be reverent in your work and keep your word, be thrifty in spending and care for the people, and call on the people for labour only at the proper times."
The Master said: "A young person should be filial at home and respectful to elders outside it; careful and trustworthy; should love all people broadly, and keep close to the humane. If any energy is left over after doing all this, then use it to study the arts and letters."
Zixia said: "If a man values worthiness more than good looks; serves his parents with all his strength; serves his lord to the point of giving his life; and in dealing with friends is true to his word - though others say he has not studied, I would certainly say that he has."
The Master said: "If a noble person is not serious, he has no authority, and what he learns will not be firm. Take loyalty and trustworthiness as your chief principles. Have no friends who are not as good as yourself. When you make a mistake, do not be afraid to correct it."
Master Zeng said: "Be careful at the end of a life and remember those long gone, and the virtue of the people will grow deeper."
Ziqin asked Zigong: "When our Master comes to a state, he always gets to hear about its government. Does he ask for it, or is it given to him?" Zigong said: "The Master gets it by being warm, good, courteous, frugal and deferential. His way of asking is surely different from other people's way of asking."
The Master said: "While a man's father is alive, look at his aims; when his father has died, look at his conduct. If for three years he does not change his father's ways, he can be called filial."
Master You said: "In the practice of ritual (li), harmony is the thing to prize. This is what made the Way of the ancient kings beautiful, and they followed it in matters great and small. Yet there are things that do not work: to know harmony and aim at harmony, without regulating it by ritual, does not work either."
Master You said: "When promises stay close to what is right, your word can be made good. When respect stays close to ritual, you keep clear of shame and disgrace. If you do not lose those you rely on, you can make them your model too."
The Master said: "A noble person does not seek a full belly when he eats, or comfort where he lives. He is quick in action and careful in speech, and goes to those who have the Way to be set straight. He can be called a lover of learning."
Zigong said: "Poor without grovelling, rich without arrogance - what about that?" The Master said: "Acceptable. But not as good as being poor and cheerful, or rich and fond of ritual." Zigong said: "The Songs say: 'As if cut, as if filed; as if carved, as if polished.' Is that what you mean?" The Master said: "Ci, now I can begin to discuss the Songs with you! I tell you what is past and you know what is to come."
The Master said: "Do not worry that others do not know you; worry that you do not know others."

keyLines.line: 學而時習之，不亦說乎
keyLines.en: To learn, and at the right times to practise what you have learnt: is that not a pleasure?
keyLines.note: The first sentence of the whole book. 「學」 is learning, and 「時習」 can mean to review at the proper times or to put into practice often; 「說」 is the same as 「悅」 (joy), the inner pleasure of having gained from study.

keyLines.line: 人不知而不慍，不亦君子乎
keyLines.en: To be unknown to others and not be resentful: is that not the mark of a noble person?
keyLines.note: Not minding that others do not understand you is the mark of the noble person. It stresses that cultivation is a matter for oneself, not for seeking recognition.

keyLines.line: 君子務本，本立而道生；孝弟也者，其為仁之本與
keyLines.en: The noble person attends to the root; when the root is established, the Way grows. Filial piety and brotherly duty: are they not the root of humaneness?
keyLines.note: The words of You Zi (a disciple of Confucius): the noble person works on the root, and once it is firm the Way arises from it. Filial and brotherly duty are the root of practising humaneness. Zhu Xi explained 'the root of humaneness' as 'practising humaneness begins with filial and brotherly duty'.

keyLines.line: 巧言令色，鮮矣仁
keyLines.en: Clever words and an ingratiating face: seldom is there humaneness in them.
keyLines.note: Smooth talk and a false look seldom go with true virtue. 「鮮」 means few.

keyLines.line: 吾日三省吾身：為人謀而不忠乎？與朋友交而不信乎？傳不習乎
keyLines.en: Each day I examine myself on three points: in doing things for others, have I been loyal? In dealings with friends, have I been trustworthy? Have I passed on what I have not practised?
keyLines.note: Zengzi (Zeng Shen, a disciple of Confucius) examined himself daily on three things: whether he had done his best for others, whether he had been honest with friends, and whether what he taught was something he had reviewed and practised.

keyLines.line: 道千乘之國，敬事而信，節用而愛人，使民以時
keyLines.en: To lead a state of a thousand chariots: be reverent in business and keep faith, be economical in expenses and love the people, and employ the people at the right seasons.
keyLines.note: How to govern a mid-sized state: act with care and keep your word, spend sparingly and love the people, and call on the people's labour without interfering with the farming seasons.

keyLines.line: 禮之用，和為貴
keyLines.en: In the practice of ritual, harmony is the most valuable thing.
keyLines.note: Another saying of You Zi. In the use of ritual, harmony is the most valuable, but 'if you do not regulate it by ritual, it also cannot work': harmony must be measured by ritual.

keyLines.line: 不患人之不己知，患不知人也
keyLines.en: Do not worry that others do not know you; worry that you do not know others.
keyLines.note: Do not fret that people do not understand you, but that you do not understand them. This echoes the saying in the first passage, 'to be unknown to others and not resentful'.

glossary.note: The same as 「悅」: joy.
In the Analects the word can mean a person of virtue or a person of rank; in this book it mostly means a person of cultivation.

glossary.en: xiao ti - 'filial piety and brotherly duty'
glossary.note: The same as 「孝悌」: obedience to parents and affection for elder brothers.
To reflect many times; 「三」 can be read as three matters or as 'several times'.

glossary.en: shen zhong zhui yuan - 'to be careful at death and remember the distant'
glossary.note: To handle the funeral of one's parents with care and remember the remote ancestors, so as to make popular custom generous.

glossary.en: qie cuo zhuo mo - 'cutting, filing, carving and polishing'
glossary.note: From the Book of Songs, in the ode 'Qi Ao' (Wei songs). It is a figure for constantly refining one's cultivation.

pian01.background: This is the first book of the Analects (Lunyu) and has long been regarded as a general introduction to the whole. Its title is taken from the first two characters of the opening saying. The books of the Analects are all named after their opening words, and the names do not summarise the content.

pian02.summary: Book 2, 'Wei zheng' (Governing), discusses rule by virtue, filial piety and study. Virtue is like the Pole Star, and teaching is better than punishment; Confucius describes the stages of his own life; filial piety needs reverence, study needs thought, and to know what you know and what you do not know is wisdom.
pian02.translation:
The Master said: "One who governs through virtue is like the North Star: it stays in its place and the other stars turn towards it."
The Master said: "The three hundred Songs can be covered in one phrase: 'Thoughts without deviation.'"
The Master said: "Lead the people with decrees and keep them in line with punishments, and they will avoid punishment but have no sense of shame. Lead them with virtue and keep them in line with ritual, and they will have a sense of shame and will also set themselves right."
The Master said: "At fifteen I set my heart on learning. At thirty I took my stand. At forty I had no doubts. At fifty I knew the mandate of Heaven. At sixty my ear was attuned. At seventy I could follow my heart's desire without overstepping the line."
Meng Yizi asked about filial piety. The Master said: "Do not disobey." Fan Chi was driving the carriage, and the Master told him: "Meng Sun asked me about filial piety and I answered, 'Do not disobey.'" Fan Chi said: "What did you mean?" The Master said: "When your parents are alive, serve them according to ritual; when they die, bury them according to ritual and sacrifice to them according to ritual."
Meng Wubo asked about filial piety. The Master said: "Let your parents have no worry except for your illness."
Ziyou asked about filial piety. The Master said: "Nowadays 'filial' means being able to feed one's parents. But even dogs and horses are fed. Without reverence, what is the difference?"
Zixia asked about filial piety. The Master said: "The hard part is the expression on your face. When there is work to do, the young take it on; when there is wine and food, they offer it to their elders. Is that all that is meant by filial piety?"
The Master said: "I talked with Hui for a whole day and he never objected, as if he were slow. But when he withdrew and I looked at how he lived on his own, he was quite able to carry my teaching further. Hui is not slow."
The Master said: "Look at what a person does. Observe the path he follows. Examine what he is at ease with. How can he hide himself? How can he hide himself?"
The Master said: "One who reviews the old and so understands the new is fit to be a teacher."
The Master said: "The noble person is not a tool."
Zigong asked about the noble person. The Master said: "He first puts his words into action, and only then lets his words follow."
The Master said: "The noble person is inclusive and not partisan; the petty person is partisan and not inclusive."
The Master said: "To learn without thinking is to be lost; to think without learning is to be in danger."
The Master said: "To work at strange doctrines does harm."
The Master said: "You, shall I teach you what knowing is? To know what you know and to know what you do not know - that is knowing."
Zizhang was learning how to seek an official salary. The Master said: "Listen widely, set aside what is doubtful, and be careful in speaking of the rest, and you will rarely be blamed. Observe widely, set aside what is risky, and be careful in acting on the rest, and you will rarely have cause for regret. When there is seldom blame in your words and seldom regret in your actions, a salary will come with it."
Duke Ai asked: "What should I do to make the people obey?" Confucius replied: "Raise up the upright and set them over the crooked, and the people will obey. Raise up the crooked and set them over the upright, and the people will not obey."
Ji Kangzi asked: "How can I make the people respectful, loyal and diligent?" The Master said: "Approach them with dignity and they will be respectful. Be filial and kind and they will be loyal. Promote the good and teach those who are not yet able, and they will be diligent."
Someone said to Confucius: "Why do you not take part in government?" The Master said: "The Book of Documents says: 'Filial, only filial, and friendly to your brothers.' If this is applied to government, that too is taking part in government. Why must one hold office to be in government?"
The Master said: "I do not see how a person without trustworthiness can get by. A big cart without a yoke-pin, a small cart without a yoke-pin - how could they go?"
Zizhang asked: "Can we know what will happen ten generations from now?" The Master said: "The Yin took over the rites of the Xia, and what it removed and added can be known. The Zhou took over the rites of the Yin, and what it removed and added can be known. Whoever may follow the Zhou, even a hundred generations on, can be known."
The Master said: "To sacrifice to spirits that are not your own is flattery. To see what is right and not do it is cowardice."

keyLines.line: 為政以德，譬如北辰，居其所，而眾星共之
keyLines.en: One who governs by virtue is like the Pole Star: it stays in its place and the multitude of stars turn towards it.
keyLines.note: To rule by virtue is like the Pole Star keeping its place while all the stars circle round it. It stresses the pull of moral example.

keyLines.line: 詩三百，一言以蔽之，曰思無邪
keyLines.en: The three hundred poems of the Book of Songs can be covered in one phrase: 'no twisted thoughts'.
keyLines.note: The three hundred poems can be summed up in one sentence as 'thoughts that are pure'. 「思無邪」 comes originally from the Book of Songs, 'Lusong', ode 'Jiong'.

keyLines.line: 道之以政，齊之以刑，民免而無恥；道之以德，齊之以禮，有恥且格
keyLines.en: Lead them by government and keep order by punishment, and the people will avoid wrong but have no sense of shame; lead them by virtue and keep order by ritual, and they will have a sense of shame and will also come to what is right.
keyLines.note: If the people are managed by decrees and punishments, they only try to stay out of punishment and do not feel shame; if they are guided by morality and ritual, they have a sense of shame and also set themselves towards good.

keyLines.line: 吾十有五而志于學；三十而立；四十而不惑；五十而知天命；六十而耳順；七十而從心所欲，不踰矩
keyLines.en: At fifteen I set my heart on learning; at thirty I took my stand; at forty I had no doubts; at fifty I knew the mandate of Heaven; at sixty my ear was attuned; at seventy I could follow my heart's desire without overstepping the line.
keyLines.note: Confucius's own account of the stages of a life of cultivation. 'No doubts' is to understand things; 'knew the mandate of Heaven' is to understand one's mission from Heaven; 'ear attuned' is to be able to take in differing views; and 'follow my heart's desire without overstepping the line' is to act freely without breaking the rules.

keyLines.line: 今之孝者，是謂能養。至於犬馬，皆能有養。不敬，何以別乎
keyLines.en: Today people call filial those who can support their parents. But even dogs and horses are supported. Without reverence, what is the difference?
keyLines.note: On filial piety: it is not only to provide for one's parents but also to have reverence in the heart; otherwise it is no different from keeping dogs and horses.

keyLines.line: 溫故而知新，可以為師矣
keyLines.en: One who reviews the old and so knows the new is fit to be a teacher.
keyLines.note: One who can review old knowledge and draw new insight from it is fit to teach.

keyLines.line: 學而不思則罔，思而不學則殆
keyLines.en: Learning without thinking is blind; thinking without learning is dangerous.
keyLines.note: To study but not think is to be bewildered; to think but not study is to be in peril. Study and thought go together.

keyLines.line: 知之為知之，不知為不知，是知也
keyLines.en: To know what you know and to know what you do not know: that is knowledge.
keyLines.note: Said to Zilu: when you know a thing, hold that you know it; when you do not know it, admit that you do not. That is true wisdom.

glossary.note: The Pole Star, which the ancients regarded as the lord of the stars.
The Book of Songs has about three hundred poems, hence 'the three hundred poems'.

glossary.en: ge - 'to come to what is right'
glossary.note: Meaning to set right, or to arrive. 「有恥且格」 means to know shame and also to return to the right path.

glossary.en: bu huo, zhi tian ming, er shun - 'no doubts, knew the mandate of Heaven, ear attuned'
glossary.note: The levels Confucius says he reached at forty, fifty and sixty.

glossary.en: jun zi bu qi - 'the noble person is not a vessel'
glossary.note: The noble person is not like a vessel with one use only; he should be broadly capable.
「罔」 is to be bewildered and gain nothing; 「殆」 is to be in doubt and in danger.

pian02.background: Most of this book is Confucius's discussion of government, filial piety and ways of learning. The passage in which he describes himself as 'at fifteen set on learning' is the one most often cited by later readers for the stages of his life and cultivation.

pian03.summary: Book 3, 'Ba yi' (The Eight Rows), is about ritual and music. It criticises the Ji family for using the Son of Heaven's music, says that the root of ritual is humaneness and reverent sincerity, and uses the saying about painting on a white ground to show that ritual comes after humaneness. It also speaks of sacrifice, music and Guan Zhong.
pian03.translation:
Confucius said of the Ji family: "They had eight rows of dancers perform in their courtyard. If this can be tolerated, what cannot be?"
The three families had the Yong ode sung as the sacrificial vessels were cleared away. The Master said: "'Assisting are the lords, and the Son of Heaven is solemn and majestic.' What place does that have in the halls of the three families?"
The Master said: "A person who lacks humaneness - what has he to do with ritual? A person who lacks humaneness - what has he to do with music?"
Lin Fang asked about the root of ritual. The Master said: "A great question! In ritual, it is better to be frugal than extravagant; in mourning, it is better to be truly grieved than to attend to every detail."
The Master said: "The barbarian tribes have their rulers, and are not like the Chinese states, which have none."
The Ji family were about to perform the lu sacrifice to Mount Tai. The Master said to Ran You: "Can you not save them?" He answered: "I cannot." The Master said: "Alas! Would you say that Mount Tai is not the equal of Lin Fang?"
The Master said: "A noble person has nothing to compete over - except perhaps archery. He bows and yields as he goes up, comes down and drinks. Even in his contest he is a noble person."
Zixia asked: "'Her sweet smile, so dimpled; her fine eyes, so clear; plain white silk for the colours' - what does this mean?" The Master said: "The painting comes after the plain ground." "Then does ritual come afterwards?" The Master said: "Shang, you lift me up! Now I can begin to discuss the Songs with you."
The Master said: "I can speak of the rites of the Xia, but the state of Qi cannot supply proof. I can speak of the rites of the Yin, but the state of Song cannot supply proof. This is because the records and the learned are not enough. If they were enough, I could use them as proof."
The Master said: "At the di sacrifice, once the libation has been poured, I do not wish to watch."
Someone asked about the explanation of the di sacrifice. The Master said: "I do not know. Whoever knew its explanation would handle the world as easily as this" - and he pointed to his palm.
"Sacrifice as if the ancestors were present; sacrifice to the spirits as if the spirits were present." The Master said: "If I do not take part in the sacrifice myself, it is as if there were no sacrifice."
Wangsun Jia asked: "'Better to court the stove than to court the south-west corner of the house' - what does that mean?" The Master said: "It is not so. One who offends Heaven has no one to pray to."
The Master said: "The Zhou looked back on the two dynasties before it, and how rich and full its culture is! I follow the Zhou."
When the Master entered the Grand Temple, he asked about everything. Someone said: "Who says the son of the man from Zou understands ritual? He enters the Grand Temple and asks about everything." The Master heard this and said: "That is itself the ritual."
The Master said: "In archery, the point is not to pierce the hide, because people's strength is not of one grade. That was the Way of the ancients."
Zigong wanted to do away with the sheep offered at the announcement of the new moon. The Master said: "Ci, you care about the sheep; I care about the ritual."
The Master said: "If you serve your lord with every point of ritual, people think you are flattering him."
Duke Ding asked: "How should a ruler employ his ministers, and how should ministers serve their ruler?" Confucius replied: "A ruler should employ his ministers with ritual; ministers should serve their ruler with loyalty."
The Master said: "The 'Guan guan' ode is joyful without being excessive, sorrowful without being wounding."
Duke Ai asked Zai Wo about the altar of the land. Zai Wo replied: "The Xia used pine, the Yin used cypress, and the Zhou used chestnut - saying, 'so as to make the people tremble.'" The Master heard of this and said: "What is done is not to be explained; what has gone ahead is not to be criticised; what is past is not to be blamed."
The Master said: "Guan Zhong was a man of small capacity!" Someone said: "Was Guan Zhong frugal?" "The Guan family held three residences, and none of his officials held two posts. How could he be called frugal?" "Then did Guan Zhong know ritual?" "A ruler has a screen at his gate, and the Guan family also had a screen at theirs. When two rulers meet in friendship, the ruler has a stand for turning over cups, and the Guan family also had one. If Guan knew ritual, who does not know ritual?"
The Master spoke to the Grand Music Master of Lu about music: "Music can be understood. It begins with the parts sounding together; then it unfolds in purity, in clarity, and in unbroken flow, until it reaches its end."
The border guard of Yi asked to see him, saying: "When noble persons have come here, I have never failed to meet them." His followers took him in to see the Master. When he came out he said: "My friends, why worry about losing office? The world has been without the Way for a long time. Heaven is going to make your Master a wooden bell-clapper."
The Master said of the Shao music: "Perfectly beautiful, and perfectly good too." He said of the Wu music: "Perfectly beautiful, but not perfectly good."
The Master said: "Rank without generosity, ritual without reverence, mourning without grief - how could I bear to look at such things?"

keyLines.line: 八佾舞於庭。是可忍也，孰不可忍也
keyLines.en: Eight rows of dancers in his courtyard! If this can be borne, what cannot be borne?
keyLines.note: The head of the Ji family had eight rows (sixty-four dancers), the full Son of Heaven's set, perform in his own courtyard. Confucius was furious: if this can be tolerated, what cannot?

keyLines.line: 人而不仁，如禮何？人而不仁，如樂何
keyLines.en: A man who is not humane, what has he to do with ritual? A man who is not humane, what has he to do with music?
keyLines.note: If a person has no humane heart, what use are ritual and music? It shows that ritual and music have humaneness as their root.

keyLines.line: 禮，與其奢也，寧儉；喪，與其易也，寧戚
keyLines.en: In ritual, better to be frugal than extravagant; in mourning, better to be grieved than merely thorough.
keyLines.note: Confucius's answer to Lin Fang's question about the root of ritual: in rites, simplicity is better than splendour; in funerals, grief is better than careful detail.

keyLines.line: 君子無所爭，必也射乎
keyLines.en: The noble person has nothing to contend for, unless it is archery.
keyLines.note: The noble person has nothing to compete over; if there is anything, it is archery, where there is bowing and yielding and the winner drinks with the loser: a contest of the noble.

keyLines.line: 繪事後素
keyLines.en: The painting comes after the plain ground.
keyLines.note: Zixia asked about the line 'plain colours make the pattern'. Confucius answered that in painting, the plain ground comes first and then the colours. From this Zixia saw that ritual comes afterwards, ritual following humaneness.

keyLines.line: 祭如在，祭神如神在
keyLines.en: Sacrifice as if present; sacrifice to the spirits as if the spirits were present.
keyLines.note: To sacrifice to ancestors as though they were before you, and to the gods as though they were there, shows the importance of reverent sincerity.

keyLines.line: 周監於二代，郁郁乎文哉！吾從周
keyLines.en: The Zhou looked back on the two dynasties before it; how rich in culture it is! I follow the Zhou.
keyLines.note: The Zhou drew on the Xia and the Shang, and its culture is abundant; I follow the Zhou system.

keyLines.line: 君使臣以禮，臣事君以忠
keyLines.en: A ruler employs his ministers by ritual; ministers serve their ruler with loyalty.
keyLines.note: Reply to Duke Ding of Lu: the ruler treats his ministers with ritual and the ministers serve him loyally.

glossary.note: The Son of Heaven's dance, eight by eight, sixty-four dancers; feudal lords had six rows and grand masters four.
The three grand-master families of Lu: Meng Sun, Shu Sun and Ji Sun.
「雍」 is the title of a Zhou ode of the Book of Songs, sung when the offerings were cleared at the Son of Heaven's sacrifice to ancestors. The Three Families used it without right.
The great sacrifice to ancestors in ancient times, performed by the Son of Heaven.

glossary.en: gao shuo zhi xi yang - 'the sacrificial sheep for announcing the new moon'
glossary.note: A rite in which a live sheep was presented at the temple on the first of each month. Zigong wanted to drop the formality, but Confucius cared for the spirit of the rite.

glossary.en: shao, wu - 'the Shao and the Wu'
glossary.note: The Shao is the music of Shun, the Wu the music of King Wu of Zhou. Confucius held the Shao to be perfect in beauty and in goodness, and the Wu beautiful but not fully good.

pian03.background: Much of this book answers the state of 'ritual in ruin and music in decay' in Lu in the Spring and Autumn period (770-476 BCE), as when the Three Families overstepped ritual. It shows Confucius's view that the root of ritual and music is humaneness, and is also important material for the study of pre-Qin ritual and music.

pian04.summary: Book 4, 'Li ren' (Dwelling in Humaneness), is about humaneness. Humaneness is the basis of conduct; the noble person cherishes virtue and understands rightness; he will not hold wealth and rank gained by wrong means; to hear the Way in the morning and die at night is enough; the Master's Way is held together by conscientiousness and reciprocity; and the book also covers serving parents and being slow in speech and quick in action.
pian04.translation:
The Master said: "It is good to live among the humane. If you choose a home that is not among the humane, how can you be called wise?"
The Master said: "Those who lack humaneness cannot stay long in hardship, and cannot stay long in comfort. The humane are at ease in humaneness; the wise find it profitable."
The Master said: "Only the humane can truly like people and truly dislike people."
The Master said: "If you set your heart on humaneness, you will have no evil in you."
The Master said: "Wealth and rank are what people want, but if they cannot be had in the right way, do not hold on to them. Poverty and low station are what people dislike, but if they cannot be escaped in the right way, do not run from them. If a noble person abandons humaneness, how can he make a name? A noble person does not depart from humaneness even for the span of a meal. In haste he keeps to it; in turmoil he keeps to it."
The Master said: "I have never seen anyone who truly loved humaneness or truly hated the inhumane. One who loves humaneness puts nothing above it. One who hates the inhumane practises humaneness, and does not let the inhumane touch him. Is there anyone who has devoted his strength to humaneness for even a single day? I have never seen anyone whose strength was not enough. Perhaps there is such a person, but I have not seen him."
The Master said: "People's faults each belong to their own kind. Look at a person's faults and you will know whether he is humane."
The Master said: "In the morning hear the Way; in the evening die content."
The Master said: "A scholar who has set his heart on the Way, yet is ashamed of poor clothes and poor food, is not worth discussing things with."
The Master said: "In the world, a noble person has no fixed 'yes' and no fixed 'no'; he goes with what is right."
The Master said: "The noble person cherishes virtue; the petty person cherishes his land. The noble person cherishes the law; the petty person cherishes favours."
The Master said: "Act always with profit in mind, and you will attract much resentment."
The Master said: "Can a state be run through ritual and yielding? Then what difficulty is there? If a state cannot be run through ritual and yielding, what use is ritual?"
The Master said: "Do not worry about having no position; worry about what you will stand on. Do not worry that no one knows you; seek to be worth knowing."
The Master said: "Shen! My Way is threaded together by one thing." Master Zeng said: "Yes." The Master went out, and the disciples asked: "What did he mean?" Master Zeng said: "The Master's Way is loyalty and reciprocity, and nothing more."
The Master said: "The noble person understands what is right; the petty person understands what is profitable."
The Master said: "When you see a worthy person, think of becoming his equal. When you see an unworthy one, look inward and examine yourself."
The Master said: "In serving your parents, remonstrate gently. If you see they are not inclined to listen, remain respectful and do not defy them; you may be worn out, but do not resent it."
The Master said: "While your parents are alive, do not travel far; and if you do travel, have a fixed destination."
The Master said: "If for three years he does not change his father's ways, he can be called filial."
The Master said: "You must know your parents' ages. On the one hand it is a reason for joy; on the other, a reason for fear."
The Master said: "In ancient times people held back their words, because they were ashamed to fall short in deed."
The Master said: "Those who hold themselves in check seldom go wrong."
The Master said: "A noble person wants to be slow in speech and quick in action."
The Master said: "Virtue is not alone; it is sure to have neighbours."
Ziyou said: "Pressing your lord too often brings disgrace. Pressing your friends too often brings distance."

keyLines.line: 里仁為美。擇不處仁，焉得知
keyLines.en: To live among the humane is good. If one chooses a home that is not among the humane, how can he be called wise?
keyLines.note: It is good to live where humaneness is; to choose a home and not choose humaneness, how can that be wise?

keyLines.line: 仁者安仁，知者利仁
keyLines.en: The humane are at rest in humaneness; the wise find humaneness profitable.
keyLines.note: The humane person is at home in humaneness; the wise person sees that it pays and practises it.

keyLines.line: 富與貴，是人之所欲也，不以其道得之，不處也
keyLines.en: Wealth and rank are what people want, but if they cannot be had in the right way, one does not stay in them.
keyLines.note: Everyone wants wealth and honour, but the noble person does not accept them if they are not gained properly.

keyLines.line: 朝聞道，夕死可矣
keyLines.en: Hear the Way in the morning, and one may die at evening.
keyLines.note: If I hear the Way in the morning, I can die in the evening. It expresses an extreme longing for truth.

keyLines.line: 君子懷德，小人懷土；君子懷刑，小人懷惠
keyLines.en: The noble person cherishes virtue; the petty person cherishes land. The noble person cherishes the law; the petty person cherishes favours.
keyLines.note: The noble person thinks of morality, the petty person of land; the noble person thinks of the law, the petty person of favours.

keyLines.line: 吾道一以貫之
keyLines.en: My Way is one thread that runs through it all.
keyLines.note: Confucius told Zeng Shen that his Way is threaded through by a single principle; Zengzi explained it as 'conscientiousness and reciprocity, that is all'.

keyLines.line: 君子喻於義，小人喻於利
keyLines.en: The noble person understands rightness; the petty person understands profit.
keyLines.note: The noble person grasps what is right; the petty person grasps what pays.

keyLines.line: 見賢思齊焉，見不賢而內自省也
keyLines.en: When you see a worthy person, think of matching him; when you see an unworthy one, look inward and examine yourself.
keyLines.note: See the good and wish to equal them; see the bad and ask whether you have the same fault.

glossary.note: To live in a neighbourhood where humane people are. Another reading takes the second character as the object of 'dwell': to dwell in humaneness.
「約」 is straitened circumstances and 「樂」 is ease and joy.
To do one's utmost is 「忠」; to extend one's own feelings to others is 「恕」. Zengzi used these two to sum up the Master's Way.
To advise one's parents mildly.
To know clearly and be well versed.

glossary.en: de bu gu, bi you lin - 'virtue is not alone; it must have neighbours'
glossary.note: A person of virtue is not isolated; he will have like-minded companions.

pian04.background: This book takes humaneness (ren) as its theme and is mostly short, maxim-like records. The saying 'my Way is one thread that runs through it all' is seen as one of the main clues to Confucius's thought.

pian05.summary: Book 5, 'Gongye Chang', judges figures from history and disciples of Confucius, among them Zigong, Zilu, Yan Hui, Zai Yu and Zichan. It gives well-known sayings such as 'quick and fond of learning, not ashamed to ask those below him' and 'listen to what he says and watch what he does'.
pian05.translation:
The Master said of Gongye Chang: "He is fit to be married. Though he was once in prison, it was not for any crime of his." And he gave him his own daughter in marriage.
The Master said of Nan Rong: "When the state has the Way, he will not be passed over; when it lacks the Way, he will escape punishment and execution." And he gave him his elder brother's daughter in marriage.
The Master said of Zijian: "What a noble person he is! If Lu had no noble persons, where could he have got it from?"
Zigong asked: "What do you think of me?" The Master said: "You are a vessel." "What sort of vessel?" "A sacrificial hu-lian vessel."
Someone said: "Yong is humane, but not eloquent." The Master said: "What use is eloquence? To meet people with a ready tongue is to be hated by them again and again. I do not know whether he is humane, but what use is eloquence?"
The Master told Qidiao Kai to take office. He replied: "I am not yet confident enough of this." The Master was pleased.
The Master said: "If the Way does not prevail, I shall take a raft and float out to sea. The one who would follow me - that would be You, would it not?" Zilu heard this and was glad. The Master said: "You has more courage than I do, but he has no way of getting the timber."
Meng Wubo asked: "Is Zilu humane?" The Master said: "I do not know." He asked again. The Master said: "As for You, in a state of a thousand chariots he could be put in charge of its military levies. I do not know whether he is humane." "And Qiu?" The Master said: "As for Qiu, in a town of a thousand households or a family of a hundred chariots, he could be made steward. I do not know whether he is humane." "And Chi?" The Master said: "As for Chi, with his sash tied on, standing at court, he could be put in charge of speaking with guests. I do not know whether he is humane."
The Master said to Zigong: "Which of you is better, you or Hui?" He answered: "How would I dare to look up to Hui? Hui hears one thing and understands ten. I hear one thing and understand two." The Master said: "You are not as good as he is. I agree with you: neither of us is as good as he is."
Zai Yu slept in the daytime. The Master said: "Rotten wood cannot be carved, and a wall of dung cannot be plastered. What is the use of scolding Yu?" The Master said: "At first, with other people, I listened to their words and trusted their deeds. Now, with other people, I listen to their words and watch their deeds. It was Yu who made me change."
The Master said: "I have not seen a man of firmness." Someone replied: "Shen Cheng." The Master said: "Cheng is full of desires. How can he be firm?"
Zigong said: "What I do not want others to do to me, I also want not to do to others." The Master said: "Ci, that is beyond you."
Zigong said: "The Master's refinements of manner and writing we can hear about. The Master's words on human nature and the Way of Heaven we cannot hear."
When Zilu had heard something and had not yet been able to put it into practice, he was afraid of hearing anything new.
Zigong asked: "Why was Kong Wenzi given the title 'Wen' (cultured)?" The Master said: "He was quick and fond of learning, and was not ashamed to ask those below him. That is why he was called 'Wen'."
The Master said of Zichan: "He had four of the ways of a noble person. He conducted himself with deference, served his superiors with respect, looked after the people with kindness, and employed the people with justice."
The Master said: "Yan Pingzhong was good at friendship: even after a long time, he still treated his friends with respect."
The Master said: "Zang Wenzhong kept a great tortoise in a house with hill-carved capitals and pond-weed painted on the roof posts. What sort of wisdom was that?"
Zizhang asked: "Ziwen, the chief minister of Chu, was made chief minister three times and showed no sign of joy; he was dismissed three times and showed no sign of anger. He always told the new chief minister about the work of the old one. What do you think of him?" The Master said: "He was loyal." "Was he humane?" "I do not know. How could that make him humane?" "When Cui Zi killed the ruler of Qi, Chen Wenzi, who had ten teams of horses, abandoned them and left. Coming to another state he said, 'They are just like our Grandee Cui.' He left. Coming to another state he said again, 'They are just like our Grandee Cui.' He left. What do you think of him?" The Master said: "He was pure." "Was he humane?" "I do not know. How could that make him humane?"
Ji Wenzi thought three times before acting. The Master heard of it and said: "Twice is enough."
The Master said: "Ning Wuzi was wise when the state had the Way, and foolish when it did not. His wisdom can be matched, but his foolishness cannot."
When the Master was in Chen, he said: "Let me go home! Let me go home! The young people of my circle are ambitious and careless; they are brilliant and have made a pattern, but they do not know how to trim it."
The Master said: "Boyi and Shuqi did not hold on to old grudges, and so they attracted little resentment."
The Master said: "Who says Weisheng Gao is upright? When someone begged vinegar from him, he begged it from a neighbour and gave it as his own."
The Master said: "Clever words, an ingratiating look, and excessive deference - Zuo Qiuming was ashamed of them, and I am ashamed of them too. Hiding resentment while befriending the person - Zuo Qiuming was ashamed of it, and I am ashamed of it too."
Yan Yuan and Jilu were attending him. The Master said: "Why does each of you not tell me what you wish for?" Zilu said: "I would like to share my carriages, horses and fur coats with my friends, and not mind if they wear them out." Yan Yuan said: "I would like not to boast of my goodness or make a show of my labours." Zilu said: "We would like to hear your wish." The Master said: "To bring peace to the old, to be trusted by friends, and to be cherished by the young."
The Master said: "It is over! I have never seen anyone who could see his own faults and bring a case against himself inwardly."
The Master said: "In a town of ten households there must be someone as loyal and trustworthy as I am, but not as fond of learning."

keyLines.line: 子謂公冶長，「可妻也
keyLines.en: The Master said of Gongye Chang that he could be given a daughter in marriage.
keyLines.note: Although Gongye Chang had been in prison, Confucius held that it was no fault of his, and gave him his daughter. Confucius judged a person by virtue, not by misfortune.

keyLines.line: 朽木不可雕也，糞土之牆，不可杇也
keyLines.en: Rotten wood cannot be carved; a wall of dung cannot be plastered.
keyLines.note: Confucius's rebuke to Zai Yu for sleeping in the daytime: rotten wood cannot be carved, and a wall of dung cannot be whitewashed.

keyLines.line: 聽其言而觀其行
keyLines.en: Listen to what he says and watch what he does.
keyLines.note: After the matter of Zai Yu, Confucius changed how he judged people: he no longer trusted conduct from words alone but watched what they did.

keyLines.line: 賜也何敢望回！回也聞一以知十，賜也聞一以知二
keyLines.en: How would I dare look up to Hui! Hui hears one thing and knows ten; I hear one thing and know two.
keyLines.note: Zigong admitted he was far behind Yan Hui, who could infer ten things from hearing one, while he could infer only two. Confucius agreed.

keyLines.line: 我不欲人之加諸我也，吾亦欲無加諸人
keyLines.en: What I do not wish others to do to me, I also wish not to do to others.
keyLines.note: Zigong's own words. Confucius replied that this was beyond him, which shows how hard the Way of reciprocity is.

keyLines.line: 敏而好學，不恥下問
keyLines.en: Quick and fond of learning, not ashamed to ask those below him.
keyLines.note: The reason Kong Wenzi was given the posthumous title 'Wen': he was sharp, loved learning, and was not ashamed to ask those of lower rank.

keyLines.line: 季文子三思而後行。子聞之曰：「再，斯可矣
keyLines.en: Ji Wenzi thought three times before acting. The Master heard of it and said: 'Twice is enough.'
keyLines.note: Ji Wenzi thought three times before he acted. Confucius said twice was enough, since too much thought leads to hesitation.

keyLines.line: 老者安之，朋友信之，少者懷之
keyLines.en: To give the old peace, to be trusted by friends, to cherish the young.
keyLines.note: Confucius's own stated aim: that the old be comforted, that friends trust one another and that the young be cared for.

glossary.note: The black ropes used to bind prisoners, meaning prison.
A precious vessel used to hold millet at ancestral sacrifices. Confucius used it to praise Zigong as a valuable talent.
Clever with words and fond of argument.
A small wooden raft.
Sleeping in the daytime; another reading takes it as 「畫寢」, painting the bedroom.
A posthumous title, here said to mean 'quick and fond of learning, not ashamed to ask those below'.

pian05.background: Much of this book is a series of judgements on people, along with how Confucius's disciples behaved. It is an important book for seeing how Confucius assessed different kinds of people and virtues.

pian06.summary: Book 6, 'Yong ye', comments on disciples such as Yan Hui, Ran Yong and Ran Qiu, and discusses the scholar who is a noble person versus the one who is petty, the balance of substance and refinement, the levels of knowing, loving and delighting, and humaneness as 'wishing to establish oneself, one establishes others'.
pian06.translation:
The Master said: "Yong could be set to face south (to rule)."
Zhonggong asked about Zisang Bozi. The Master said: "He is acceptable - he is relaxed." Zhonggong said: "To be reverent in one's attitude and relaxed in one's practice when facing the people - is that not acceptable? But to be relaxed in attitude and relaxed in practice - is that not too relaxed?" The Master said: "What Yong says is right."
Duke Ai asked: "Which of your disciples is fond of learning?" Confucius replied: "There was Yan Hui, who was fond of learning. He did not vent his anger on others, and he did not repeat a mistake. Unfortunately his life was short and he died. Now there is no one, and I have not heard of anyone who is fond of learning."
Zihua was sent on a mission to Qi, and Ran Zi asked for grain for his mother. The Master said: "Give her a fu." He asked for more. "Give her a yu." Ran Zi gave her five bing. The Master said: "When Chi went to Qi, he rode fat horses and wore light furs. I have heard it said: a noble person helps the needy, not the rich."
Yuan Si was made steward and was given nine hundred measures of grain, and declined. The Master said: "Do not! Could you not give it to your neighbours and the people of your district?"
The Master said of Zhonggong: "If the calf of a plough ox is reddish and has good horns, though people may not want to use it, would the spirits of the mountains and rivers pass it by?"
The Master said: "Hui's heart did not stray from humaneness for three months. The others reach it only for a day or a month, and that is all."
Ji Kangzi asked: "Could Zhong You be given a post in government?" The Master said: "You is resolute. What difficulty would he have in government?" "Could Ci be given a post in government?" "Ci is far-sighted. What difficulty would he have in government?" "Could Qiu be given a post in government?" "Qiu is talented. What difficulty would he have in government?"
The Ji family wanted to make Min Ziqian steward of Bi. Min Ziqian said: "Please decline for me, politely. If anyone comes back to ask me again, I shall certainly be on the banks of the Wen."
Boniu was ill, and the Master went to ask after him. Holding his hand through the window, he said: "He is dying. It is fate! Such a man, and such an illness! Such a man, and such an illness!"
The Master said: "How worthy Hui is! A bamboo bowl of rice, a gourd of water, living in a back alley - other people could not bear the hardship, but Hui does not let it change his joy. How worthy Hui is!"
Ran Qiu said: "It is not that I do not delight in your Way, but my strength is not enough." The Master said: "Those whose strength is not enough give up halfway. You are drawing the line yourself."
The Master said to Zixia: "Be a noble scholar (ru), not a petty scholar."
Ziyou was steward of Wucheng. The Master said: "Have you found good people there?" He said: "There is a man called Tantai Mieming. He does not take shortcuts when he walks, and unless it is public business he has never come to my room."
The Master said: "Meng Zhifan does not boast. When the army fled he stayed in the rear, and as he was about to enter the gate he whipped his horse and said, 'It was not that I dared to stay behind; my horse would not go forward.'"
The Master said: "Without the glib tongue of Priest Tuo, or the good looks of Prince Zhao of Song, it is hard to escape harm in the world today."
The Master said: "Who can go out except by the door? Why does no one follow this Way?"
The Master said: "When substance wins over refinement, the result is rustic; when refinement wins over substance, the result is a clerk. Only when refinement and substance are balanced do you have a noble person."
The Master said: "People live by being upright. The one who lives without it escapes only by luck."
The Master said: "Those who know it are not equal to those who love it, and those who love it are not equal to those who delight in it."
The Master said: "To people above the middle, you can speak of higher things. To people below the middle, you cannot speak of higher things."
Fan Chi asked about wisdom. The Master said: "Devote yourself to what is right for the people; respect the spirits, but keep them at a distance. That can be called wisdom." He asked about humaneness. The Master said: "The humane person takes the hard part first and the reward afterwards. That can be called humaneness."
The Master said: "The wise delight in water; the humane delight in mountains. The wise are active; the humane are still. The wise are happy; the humane live long."
The Master said: "If Qi changed once, it would reach the level of Lu; if Lu changed once, it would reach the Way."
The Master said: "A gu that is not a gu - what a gu! What a gu!"
Zai Wo asked: "If someone told a humane person, 'There is a person in the well,' would he go in after him?" The Master said: "Why would he do that? A noble person can be made to go there, but cannot be made to fall in. He can be deceived, but he cannot be fooled."
The Master said: "The noble person who studies widely in literature and keeps himself in check with ritual will not go astray."
The Master visited Nanzi, and Zilu was displeased. The Master swore: "If I have done anything wrong, may Heaven reject me! May Heaven reject me!"
The Master said: "As a virtue, the Mean is surely the highest! Yet it has been rare among the people for a long time."
Zigong said: "If someone gave widely to the people and could help the multitude, what would you say? Could he be called humane?" The Master said: "Why only humane? He would surely be a sage! Even Yao and Shun would find that hard. A humane person, wanting to establish himself, establishes others; wanting to succeed, helps others to succeed. To be able to take what is near as an example - that can be called the method of humaneness."

keyLines.line: 雍也，可使南面
keyLines.en: Yong could be set facing south.
keyLines.note: Praise of Ran Yong as having the talent and virtue to be a ruler. A ruler sat facing south.

keyLines.line: 有顏回者，好學；不遷怒，不貳過
keyLines.en: There was one called Yan Hui who loved learning: he did not vent his anger on others, and he did not repeat a mistake.
keyLines.note: Confucius praised Yan Hui's love of learning: he did not pass his anger to others, and he did not make the same mistake twice.

keyLines.line: 賢哉回也！一簞食，一瓢飮，在陋巷，人不堪其憂，回也不改其樂
keyLines.en: How worthy Hui is! A basket of rice, a gourd of water, living in a mean alley: others could not bear the hardship, but Hui does not change his joy.
keyLines.note: In admiration of Yan Hui's joy in poverty and the Way: with a basket of rice, a gourd of water and a mean alley to live in, others could not bear it, but Hui's happiness did not change.

keyLines.line: 女為君子儒，無為小人儒
keyLines.en: You should be a noble Confucian, not a petty Confucian.
keyLines.note: A warning to Zixia to be a scholar who values moral cultivation, not one who cares only for gain or form.

keyLines.line: 質勝文則野，文勝質則史。文質彬彬，然後君子
keyLines.en: When substance outweighs refinement, one is rough; when refinement outweighs substance, one is a clerk. Only when substance and refinement are well balanced is one a noble person.
keyLines.note: If plainness outweighs polish the result is crude; if polish outweighs plainness it is showy, like a scribe. Only when the two are in due proportion is one a noble person.

keyLines.line: 知之者，不如好之者，好之者，不如樂之者
keyLines.en: To know it is not as good as to love it; to love it is not as good as to delight in it.
keyLines.note: Knowing is not as good as loving, and loving is not as good as delighting in it: three levels of learning.

keyLines.line: 務民之義，敬鬼神而遠之，可謂知矣
keyLines.en: To work at what is right for the people, and to respect the spirits while keeping them at a distance, can be called wisdom.
keyLines.note: The answer to Fan Chi's question about wisdom: devote oneself to what the people are due, and revere the spirits but keep a distance from them.

keyLines.line: 夫仁者，己欲立而立人，己欲達而達人。能近取譬，可謂仁之方也已
keyLines.en: The humane person, wishing to establish himself, establishes others; wishing to get through, gets others through. To be able to draw from what is near at hand: this may be called the method of humaneness.
keyLines.note: One who wants to stand firm helps others stand firm, and one who wants to get through helps others get through. To take examples from what is near at hand is the way to practise humaneness.

glossary.note: In old times the ruler sat facing south to hear affairs of state, so the phrase means the throne.

glossary.en: bu qian nu, bu er guo - 'not venting anger, not repeating mistakes'
glossary.note: Not moving one's anger onto others, and not committing the same error again.

glossary.en: yi dan shi, yi piao yin - 'a basket of rice, a gourd of water'
glossary.note: A 「簞」 is a bamboo basket for rice and a 「瓢」 a dipper made from a split gourd; it describes a plain life.
Originally a person who studied ritual and music; Confucius divided them into the noble and the petty.

glossary.term: 中庸之為德也，其至矣乎
glossary.en: zhong yong zhi wei de ye, qi zhi yi hu - 'the mean as a virtue, surely the highest'
glossary.note: The term 'mean' appears here, and the title of the Doctrine of the Mean is related to it.

glossary.en: bo shi ji zhong - 'to give widely and help the multitude'
glossary.note: To give widely and relieve the many; Confucius thought that even Yao and Shun would hardly be able to do this fully.

pian06.background: This book mentions 'the mean as a virtue', the only passage in the Analects to speak directly of the 'mean' (zhongyong); it later became one of the sources of the thought of the Doctrine of the Mean.

pian07.summary: Book 7, 'Shu er', shows Confucius's picture of himself: to transmit and not create, to love the ancients and seek diligently, to teach tirelessly, to forget food in his zeal and his worries in his joy. It also covers methods of teaching, attitudes to life and the temperament of the noble person.
pian07.translation:
The Master said: "I transmit and do not create. I trust in the ancients and love them. In this I venture to compare myself with our old Peng."
The Master said: "To remember in silence what I learn, to study without tiring, to teach others without weariness - which of these do I truly have?"
The Master said: "That I do not cultivate virtue, that I do not work at what I learn, that I hear what is right and cannot move towards it, that I cannot correct what is not good in me - these are what worry me."
When the Master was at leisure at home, he was relaxed and cheerful.
The Master said: "How far I have declined! It is a long time since I last dreamed of the Duke of Zhou."
The Master said: "Set your heart on the Way, hold fast to virtue, lean on humaneness, and take your leisure in the arts."
The Master said: "From anyone who has brought me a bundle of dried meat or more, I have never withheld teaching."
The Master said: "I do not open up the matter for someone who is not eager; I do not give a word to someone who is not struggling to speak. If I raise one corner and he cannot come back with the other three, I do not teach him again."
When the Master ate beside someone in mourning, he never ate his fill. On a day when he had wept, he did not sing.
The Master said to Yan Yuan: "When employed, to go ahead; when set aside, to withdraw into oneself - only you and I can do that." Zilu said: "If you were leading the three armies, whom would you take with you?" The Master said: "I would not take someone who would fight a tiger bare-handed or cross a river on foot and die without regret. I would take someone who approaches a task with caution and likes to plan so as to bring it off."
The Master said: "If wealth could be sought, even if it meant being a groom with a whip, I would do it. But if it cannot be sought, I shall follow what I love."
What the Master was careful about: fasting before sacrifices, war, and illness.
The Master heard the Shao music in Qi and for three months did not notice the taste of meat. He said: "I never imagined that music could reach such heights."
Ran You said: "Is the Master on the side of the ruler of Wei?" Zigong said: "Well, I shall ask him." He went in and said: "What sort of men were Boyi and Shuqi?" "Worthy men of old." "Did they resent it?" "They sought humaneness and found humaneness. Why should they resent it?" He came out and said: "The Master is not on his side."
The Master said: "Coarse rice to eat, water to drink, a bent arm for a pillow - there is joy in this too. Wealth and rank gained by wrong means are to me like floating clouds."
The Master said: "If I were given a few more years, so that I could study the Changes from the age of fifty, I could avoid making great mistakes."
What the Master spoke in the standard speech: the Songs, the Documents, and the practice of ritual. All of these he spoke in the standard speech.
The Lord of She asked Zilu about Confucius, and Zilu did not answer. The Master said: "Why did you not say: 'He is the kind of man who forgets to eat in his eagerness, forgets his worries in his joy, and does not notice that old age is coming on'?"
The Master said: "I was not born knowing. I am someone who loves the ancients and is quick to seek knowledge from them."
The Master did not speak of prodigies, force, disorder or spirits.
The Master said: "Walking along with two other people, I am bound to find a teacher among them. I pick out their good points and follow them, and their bad points and correct them in myself."
The Master said: "Heaven has given me virtue. What can Huan Tui do to me?"
The Master said: "My friends, do you think I am hiding something from you? I hide nothing from you. There is nothing I do that I do not share with you, my friends. That is the sort of person I am."
The Master taught four things: literature, conduct, loyalty and trustworthiness.
The Master said: "I shall not get to see a sage. If I could see a noble person, that would be enough." The Master said: "I shall not get to see a good person. If I could see someone with constancy, that would be enough. To have nothing and pretend to have, to be empty and pretend to be full, to be pinched and pretend to be comfortable - it is hard for such people to have constancy."
The Master fished with a rod but not with a net, and shot with an arrow but not at roosting birds.
The Master said: "There may be people who act without knowing, but I am not one of them. To listen widely, pick out what is good and follow it; to see widely and remember it - that is the next best thing to knowing."
It was hard to talk with the people of Huxiang. A boy from there was received by the Master, and the disciples were puzzled. The Master said: "I approve of his coming forward, not of his holding back. Why be so harsh? When someone purifies himself in order to come forward, approve of his purification; do not hold on to his past."
The Master said: "Is humaneness far away? If I want humaneness, humaneness is here."
The judge of Chen asked: "Did Duke Zhao know ritual?" Confucius answered: "He knew ritual." Confucius withdrew, and the judge bowed to Wuma Qi to bring him forward, and said: "I have heard that the noble person is not partisan. Is the noble person partisan too? The Duke took a wife from Wu, of the same surname as himself, and called her 'Mengzi of Wu'. If the Duke knew ritual, who does not know ritual?" Wuma Qi reported this. The Master said: "How fortunate I am! If I make a mistake, others are sure to know of it."
When the Master sang with others and they sang well, he would have them sing it again, and then join in.
The Master said: "In literary learning I may be about the equal of others, but I have not yet achieved the conduct of a noble person."
The Master said: "As for being a sage or humane - how would I dare claim that? What can be said of me is that I do it without tiring and teach others without weariness." Gongxi Hua said: "That is exactly what we disciples cannot learn."
The Master was seriously ill, and Zilu asked to offer prayers. The Master said: "Is there such a practice?" Zilu answered: "There is. The eulogy says: 'We pray for you to the spirits above and below.'" The Master said: "Then I have been praying for a long time."
The Master said: "Extravagance leads to arrogance, and frugality leads to meanness. Better to be mean than arrogant."
The Master said: "The noble person is open and at ease; the petty person is always worried and anxious."
The Master was gentle yet strict, dignified yet not fierce, respectful yet at ease.

keyLines.line: 述而不作，信而好古，竊比於我老彭
keyLines.en: I transmit and do not create; I trust and love the ancients; I privately compare myself to old Peng.
keyLines.note: Confucius on himself: he hands on rather than invents, he believes in and loves ancient culture, and he quietly compares himself to Lao Peng (a worthy minister of the Yin).

keyLines.line: 默而識之，學而不厭，誨人不倦，何有於我哉
keyLines.en: To remember in silence what I learn, to study without tiring, to teach others without weariness: which of these have I managed?
keyLines.note: To quietly keep what he learns, never tire of study and never weary of teaching: how many of these does he have? It shows his modesty and self-scrutiny.

keyLines.line: 不憤不啟；不悱不發
keyLines.en: I do not enlighten one who is not eager; I do not help out one who is not struggling to speak.
keyLines.note: He does not guide a student until the student has struggled and cannot solve the problem, and does not prompt until the student wants to say it and cannot. The later word for 'to inspire' comes from this.

keyLines.line: 飯疏食，飮水，曲肱而枕之，樂亦在其中矣。不義而富且貴，於我如浮雲
keyLines.en: Eating coarse rice and drinking water, with my bent arm for a pillow, I still find joy in it. Wealth and rank gained by wrong means are to me like floating clouds.
keyLines.note: Even with plain rice, water and an arm for a pillow, there is joy; riches and honour gained unrighteously are like drifting clouds to me.

keyLines.line: 其為人也，發憤忘食，樂以忘憂，不知老之將至云爾
keyLines.en: He is the sort of man who in his eagerness forgets his food, in his joy forgets his worries, and does not notice that old age is coming on.
keyLines.note: Confucius's description of himself: absorbed in his work he forgets to eat, in his joy he forgets his cares, and he does not know that old age is coming.

keyLines.line: 三人行，必有我師焉
keyLines.en: When three people walk together, there is bound to be a teacher for me among them.
keyLines.note: When several people walk together, one of them is sure to be someone I can learn from; I take what is good and use what is not good as a warning.

keyLines.line: 子以四教：文、行、忠、信
keyLines.en: The Master taught four things: culture, conduct, loyalty and good faith.
keyLines.note: The four subjects of Confucius's teaching: literature, moral conduct, loyalty and trustworthiness.

keyLines.line: 仁遠乎哉？我欲仁，斯仁至矣
keyLines.en: Is humaneness far away? If I wish to be humane, humaneness is at hand.
keyLines.note: Is humaneness far from us? If I want it, it comes. It stresses that humaneness comes from one's own awareness.

glossary.note: Some take him to be Peng Zu, a worthy minister of the Shang (Yin) dynasty; others take it to mean the two men Lao Dan and Peng Zu. Views have always differed.

glossary.en: shu xiu - 'a bundle of dried meat'
glossary.note: A bundle of dried meat, a small gift for a teacher in ancient times; it stands for the humblest present.

glossary.en: san yu fan - 'to come back with the other three corners'
glossary.note: To infer the other three corners from one; the idiom 'from one, infer three' comes from this.
The standard language of the time. Confucius used it when he recited the Songs and Documents and performed rites, rather than a dialect.

glossary.en: zi bu yu guai li luan shen - 'the Master did not speak of marvels, force, disorder or spirits'
glossary.note: Confucius did not talk about strange things, feats of strength, disorder, or ghosts and spirits.

glossary.term: 志於道，據於德，依於仁，游於藝
glossary.en: zhi yu dao, ju yu de, yi yu ren, you yu yi - 'set the will on the Way, rest on virtue, lean on humaneness, wander in the arts'
glossary.note: The order and range of cultivation: take the Way as one's aim, virtue as one's basis, humaneness as one's support, and roam freely among the six arts.

pian07.background: This book mostly records Confucius's words, conduct and temperament, and is important for understanding his personal image and his ideas of teaching. 'Transmitting and not creating' is seen as Confucius's own account of his scholarly work.

pian08.summary: Book 8, 'Tai Bo', praises Tai Bo and the virtue of Yao, Shun and Yu, records the last words of Zengzi, speaks of the breadth and resolution of the scholar, of being roused by poetry, set up by ritual and completed by music, and says 'if one is not in the post, one does not plan its affairs'.
pian08.translation:
The Master said: "Taibo may be said to have reached the highest virtue. Three times he gave up the world, and the people found no way to praise him."
The Master said: "Respect without ritual becomes exhausting; caution without ritual becomes timidity; courage without ritual becomes disorder; frankness without ritual becomes harshness. When a noble person is generous to his kin, the people rise towards humaneness. When he does not forget old friends, the people do not turn mean."
When Master Zeng was ill, he called his disciples and said: "Uncover my feet! Uncover my hands! The Songs say: 'Trembling, wary, as if standing at the edge of a deep pool, as if treading on thin ice.' From now on, I know I am out of danger, my young friends!"
When Master Zeng was ill, Meng Jingzi went to ask after him. Master Zeng said: "When a bird is about to die, its cry is mournful; when a person is about to die, his words are good. In the Way, a noble person values three things: in bearing and manner, to keep clear of violence and arrogance; in his expression, to stay close to sincerity; in his speech and tone, to keep clear of coarseness and error. As for the matter of the ritual vessels, there are officials for that."
Master Zeng said: "Though able, to ask those who are not; though knowing much, to ask those who know little; to have, yet seem to have nothing; to be full, yet seem empty; to be offended against, yet not retaliate - long ago a friend of mine practised this."
Master Zeng said: "One who can be trusted with an orphan prince only six feet tall, who can be entrusted with the fate of a state of a hundred li, and who cannot be shaken in a great crisis - is he a noble person? He is a noble person indeed."
Master Zeng said: "A scholar must be broad-minded and resolute, for his burden is heavy and his road is long. He takes humaneness as his burden - is that not heavy? Only with death does he put it down - is that not long?"
The Master said: "Be stirred by the Songs, take your stand through ritual, and be completed by music."
The Master said: "The people can be made to follow a path, but cannot be made to understand why."
The Master said: "Someone who loves courage and hates poverty will cause disorder. A person who lacks humaneness, if you hate him too much, will cause disorder."
The Master said: "Even if someone had the Duke of Zhou's talents and gifts, if he was arrogant and mean, the rest would not be worth looking at."
The Master said: "It is not easy to find someone who has studied for three years and has no thought of a salary."
The Master said: "Hold firmly to faith and love learning; guard the good Way even to death. Do not enter a state in danger, do not stay in a state in disorder. When the world has the Way, appear; when it lacks the Way, withdraw. When the state has the Way, to be poor and lowly is shameful; when the state lacks the Way, to be rich and honoured is shameful."
The Master said: "If you do not hold the position, do not plan its policy."
The Master said: "When Music Master Zhi began, and in the finale of the 'Guan guan' - how rich and full it was, filling the ears!"
The Master said: "I do not understand people who are wild but not straightforward, simple but not honest, earnest but not trustworthy."
The Master said: "Learn as if you could never catch up, and as if afraid of losing what you have."
The Master said: "How lofty! Shun and Yu possessed the world and took no part in seeking it."
The Master said: "How great Yao was as a ruler! How lofty! Only Heaven is great, and only Yao took it as his model. How vast! The people could find no name for it. How lofty were his achievements! How brilliant were his cultural works!"
Shun had five ministers, and the world was well ordered. King Wu said: "I have ten ministers who bring order." Confucius said: "'Talent is hard to find' - is that not so? The time of Tang and Yu was the richest, and yet among the ten there was a woman, so there were only nine men. King Wen held two thirds of the world and still served the Yin. The virtue of the Zhou may be called the highest virtue indeed."
The Master said: "I can find no fault in Yu. He ate and drank simply, yet gave his utmost to the spirits; he wore coarse clothes, yet his sacrificial apron and cap were of the finest; he lived in a low house, yet gave all his strength to the irrigation channels. I can find no fault in Yu."

keyLines.line: 泰伯，其可謂至德也已矣！三以天下讓
keyLines.en: Tai Bo may be said to have had the highest virtue! Three times he gave up the world.
keyLines.note: Tai Bo gave the kingdom to his younger brother three times, so quietly that the people could find no words to praise him: the highest virtue.

keyLines.line: 恭而無禮則勞，慎而無禮則葸，勇而無禮則亂，直而無禮則絞
keyLines.en: Reverence without ritual is wearying; caution without ritual is timid; courage without ritual is disorder; frankness without ritual is harsh.
keyLines.note: Respect, care, courage and candour, without ritual to regulate them, turn respectively into fatigue, timidity, disorder and harshness.

keyLines.line: 戰戰兢兢，如臨深淵，如履薄冰
keyLines.en: In fear and trembling, as if on the brink of an abyss, as if treading on thin ice.
keyLines.note: Zengzi, near death, quoted the Book of Songs to describe his lifelong care to keep his body whole. It is the source of the idiom.

keyLines.line: 士不可以不弘毅，任重而道遠
keyLines.en: A scholar must be broad and resolute, for the burden is heavy and the road long.
keyLines.note: A scholar must be broad-minded and strong-willed, because the load is heavy and the way is long.

keyLines.line: 仁以為己任，不亦重乎；死而後已，不亦遠乎
keyLines.en: He takes humaneness as his own burden; is it not heavy? Only with death does it end; is it not long?
keyLines.note: To take realising humaneness as one's own task is heavy indeed, and to carry on until death is a long road.

keyLines.line: 興於詩，立於禮，成於樂
keyLines.en: Be roused by the Songs, set up by ritual, completed by music.
keyLines.note: The three stages of cultivation: inspiration from poetry, a footing from ritual, and fulfilment from music.

keyLines.line: 民可使由之，不可使知之
keyLines.en: The people may be made to follow it, but may not be made to understand it.
keyLines.note: Commonly read as: the people can be led to follow the Way but cannot be made to understand all its reasons. Some punctuate it as 'if the people can, let them follow; if they cannot, let them be made to understand'.

keyLines.line: 不在其位，不謀其政
keyLines.en: If one is not in the post, one does not plan its affairs.
keyLines.note: If you do not hold a post, do not meddle in its government.

glossary.note: The greatest virtue.
Fearful, afraid.
Speaking in a sharp and hurtful way.
Wide of mind and firm of will.
The master musician of Lu, whose name was Zhi.

glossary.en: guan ju zhi luan - 'the finale of Guan Ju'
glossary.note: 「亂」 is the final section of a piece of music, here the ensemble finale of the ode 'Guan Ju'.

pian08.background: This book mostly records the words and deeds of Zengzi and praise of the sage-kings of antiquity, which reflects the stress of Confucius's later followers on self-cultivation and handing down the tradition. The line 'the people may be made to follow it, but may not be made to understand it' has been punctuated and explained in different ways through the ages.

pian09.summary: Book 9, 'Zi han', records Confucius's way of dealing with the world and his teaching: cutting off four faults, being in danger at Kuang, saying he knows nothing, and Yan Yuan's sigh that 'the more I look up at it, the higher it is'. It contains famous lines such as 'what passes is like this river', 'in the cold of the year we see the pine and cypress' and 'the commander of three armies can be taken'.
pian09.translation:
The Master rarely spoke of profit, of fate, or of humaneness.
A man of Daxiang village said: "How great Confucius is! He has learned so widely, and yet there is nothing he is known for." The Master heard of this and said to his disciples: "What shall I take up? Charioteering? Archery? I shall take up charioteering."
The Master said: "A hemp cap is what ritual prescribes. Nowadays people use silk, which is thrifty, and I go along with the majority. To bow below the hall is what ritual prescribes. Nowadays people bow above it, which is presumptuous. Though it goes against the majority, I follow bowing below."
The Master was free of four things: he had no guesswork, no insistence, no stubbornness, and no self.
The Master was held in fear at Kuang. He said: "King Wen is dead, but is his culture not here with me? If Heaven meant this culture to perish, a later mortal like me would not have been able to take part in it. If Heaven does not mean this culture to perish, what can the men of Kuang do to me?"
The grand steward asked Zigong: "Is your Master a sage? How many things he can do!" Zigong said: "Certainly Heaven has let him become a sage, and he can do many things as well." The Master heard of this and said: "Does the grand steward know me? I was poor when I was young, so I learned many humble skills. Does a noble person have many? He does not need many."
Lao said: "The Master said: 'I was not employed, so I learned skills.'"
The Master said: "Do I have knowledge? I have none. When a simple man asks me something and his mind is quite blank, I take up both ends of the question and go through it to the end."
The Master said: "The phoenix does not come, the river gives out no chart - it is over for me!"
When the Master saw someone in mourning dress, someone in ceremonial cap and robes, or someone blind, he would rise on seeing them, even if they were younger, and when passing them he would hurry.
Yan Yuan sighed and said: "The more I look up at it, the higher it is; the more I bore into it, the harder it is. I see it in front of me, and suddenly it is behind. The Master leads one on step by step, with skill. He broadens me with literature and holds me in check with ritual. I want to stop and cannot. When I have used up all my strength, something seems to stand there sharp and clear. I want to follow it, but there is no way."
The Master was seriously ill, and Zilu had the disciples act as his retainers. When the illness eased, the Master said: "It is a long time that You has been playing false! Having no retainers and pretending to have them - whom do I deceive? Do I deceive Heaven? And besides, would I not rather die in the hands of you, my friends, than in the hands of retainers? Even if I do not get a grand funeral, I will not be left to die by the roadside."
Zigong said: "Here is a beautiful piece of jade. Should I wrap it in a box and store it, or look for a good price and sell it?" The Master said: "Sell it! Sell it! I am waiting for a buyer."
The Master wanted to live among the nine eastern tribes. Someone said: "They are crude. How could you live there?" The Master said: "If a noble person lived there, what crudeness would there be?"
The Master said: "After I came back from Wei to Lu, the music was put right, and the Ya and the Song each found their proper place."
The Master said: "Abroad, to serve dukes and ministers; at home, to serve father and elder brothers; not to dare to be slack in mourning; not to be overcome by wine - what difficulty are these for me?"
The Master stood by a river and said: "What passes is like this, is it not? It does not stop, day or night."
The Master said: "I have never seen anyone who loves virtue as much as he loves beauty."
The Master said: "It is like building a mound: if I stop one basket short of completion, it is I who have stopped. It is like levelling ground: even if I have tipped in only one basket, if I go on, it is I who have gone on."
The Master said: "Hui is the one who listened to me without flagging."
The Master said of Yan Yuan: "What a pity! I saw him advance; I never saw him stop."
The Master said: "There are sprouts that never flower, are there not? There are flowers that never bear fruit, are there not?"
The Master said: "The young are to be held in awe. How do we know that those who come after will not be the equal of those now? But if at forty or fifty they have not been heard of, then they are not to be held in awe."
The Master said: "Can anyone fail to follow words of correct advice? What matters is to change. Can anyone fail to be pleased by words of gentle encouragement? What matters is to think them through. If someone is pleased and does not think it through, follows and does not change, there is nothing I can do for him."
The Master said: "Take loyalty and trustworthiness as your chief principles. Have no friends who are not as good as yourself. When you make a mistake, do not be afraid to correct it."
The Master said: "The commander of three armies can be taken from them, but the will of an ordinary man cannot be taken from him."
The Master said: "Dressed in a worn quilted gown and standing beside people in fox and badger furs, without feeling ashamed - that would be You. 'Not envious, not greedy, how could he not be good?'" Zilu recited this for the rest of his life. The Master said: "That Way alone - how is that enough to be good?"
The Master said: "Only when the year turns cold do we know that the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves."
The Master said: "The wise are not confused; the humane do not worry; the brave are not afraid."
The Master said: "There are people with whom you can study but not yet go along the Way; people with whom you can go along the Way but not yet take your stand; people with whom you can take your stand but not yet weigh circumstances."
"The flowers of the wild plum, how they flutter and turn! Do I not think of you? But your house is far away." The Master said: "He did not really think of her. If he did, what distance would there be?"

keyLines.line: 子絕四：「毋意，毋必，毋固，毋我
keyLines.en: The Master cut off four things: no conjecture, no insistence, no stubbornness, no egoism.
keyLines.note: Confucius was free of four faults: not guessing, not being dogmatic, not being obstinate, and not being self-centred.

keyLines.line: 文王既沒，文不在茲乎？天之將喪斯文也
keyLines.en: King Wen is dead, but is not his culture here with me? If Heaven meant to destroy this culture...
keyLines.note: When he was besieged at Kuang, Confucius was sure that this culture was carried by him: if Heaven did not mean to destroy it, the men of Kuang could do nothing to him.

keyLines.line: 仰之彌高，鑽之彌堅，瞻之在前，忽焉在後
keyLines.en: The more I look up at it, the higher it is; the more I drill into it, the harder it is; I see it in front, and suddenly it is behind.
keyLines.note: Yan Yuan's sigh at his teacher's Way: looking up, it seems higher; delving, it seems harder; it appears in front and suddenly is behind: how lofty and unfathomable the Way is.

keyLines.line: 逝者如斯夫！不舍晝夜
keyLines.en: What passes is like this river, never ceasing day or night!
keyLines.note: Confucius sighed by a river that what passes is just like this water, going on night and day. Later ages have used it to lament the passing of time.

keyLines.line: 吾未見好德如好色者也
keyLines.en: I have not seen anyone who loves virtue as he loves beauty.
keyLines.note: I have never seen anyone who loves virtue as much as he loves a beautiful face.

keyLines.line: 後生可畏，焉知來者之不如今也
keyLines.en: The young are to be held in awe; how do you know that those to come will not match the present?
keyLines.note: Young people deserve respect; who is to say that those who come later will not equal us now?
