keyLines.line: 三軍可奪帥也，匹夫不可奪志也
keyLines.en: The commander of the three armies can be taken away, but the will of a common man cannot be taken away.
keyLines.note: The general of three armies can be seized, but the resolve of an ordinary man cannot.

keyLines.line: 歲寒，然後知松柏之後凋也
keyLines.en: Only when the year grows cold do we see that the pine and cypress are the last to fade.
keyLines.note: Only in the cold season do we see that the pine and cypress are the last to wither: a figure for integrity showing itself in hardship.

glossary.en: zi han yan li yu ming yu ren - 'the Master rarely spoke of profit, fate and humaneness'
glossary.note: Confucius rarely spoke about profit, fate and humaneness. One reading takes 「與」 as 'approved of', meaning he approved of fate and humaneness.
A place name. Passing through Kuang, Confucius was taken for Yang Hu and was besieged.

glossary.en: feng niao, he tu - 'the phoenix and the river chart'
glossary.note: In old legends, signs of good omen when a sage-king appeared. Confucius sighed that no sage-king arose.

glossary.en: yun du - 'to keep in a casket'
glossary.note: To be kept in a box.
To sell: 'looking for a good price to sell' means waiting for someone who knows its worth.
Weighing circumstances: being able to adapt with the times without losing the Way.

pian09.background: The title is taken from the opening words, 'The Master rarely spoke of...'. The text is short but full of fine lines, such as 'what passes is like this river', 'pine and cypress in the cold' and 'a common man's will cannot be taken', which have often been taken up in calligraphy and as personal mottoes.

pian10.summary: Book 10, 'Xiang dang', describes Confucius's bearing and conduct at court, in his village, at sacrifices, in eating, dress and daily life, showing a life in which he kept to ritual and yet was natural and in measure.
pian10.translation:
In his home village Confucius was gentle and deferential, like someone who could not speak. In the ancestral temple and at court he spoke fluently, but with care.
At court, when he spoke with junior grandees he was easy and direct; with senior grandees he was upright and precise. When the ruler was present, he was reverent yet composed.
When the ruler summoned him to receive guests, his expression took on a look of alertness and his steps quickened. He bowed to those standing with him, to the left and to the right, and the front and back of his robe hung straight. As he hurried forward, his arms were spread like wings. When the guests had gone, he always reported back: "The guest is no longer looking back."
On entering the ruler's gate he bent low, as if there were no room to pass. He did not stand in the middle of the gateway and did not step on the threshold. Passing the ruler's place, his expression took on a look of alertness, his steps quickened, and his words seemed to come from someone short of breath. Lifting the hem of his robe to go up into the hall, he bent low and held his breath as if not breathing. On coming out, after descending one step, he relaxed his face and looked at ease. At the foot of the steps he hurried forward with his arms like wings. Back at his place, he was again reverent and composed.
Holding the jade tablet, he bent low as if he could not bear its weight. He held it up as if bowing, and down as if handing something over. His face looked tense as if trembling, and his feet shuffled as if following a line. At the presentation of gifts, his face was pleasant; at the private audience, he was relaxed.
The noble person did not use deep blue or purplish-black for trimming, and did not use red or purple for everyday clothes. In hot weather he wore an unlined garment of fine or coarse hemp, but always with an outer garment over it. Over black he wore lambskin, over white fawn, over yellow fox. His everyday fur coat was long, with the right sleeve short. He always had a sleeping garment, one and a half times his body in length. He used thick fox and badger fur for sitting at home. Once mourning was over, he wore every kind of ornament. Unless it was a court apron, his garments were always cut narrow. He did not wear lambskin and a black cap to pay condolence calls. On the first day of the month he always put on court dress and went to court.
When fasting, he always wore a clean garment of cloth. When fasting, he always changed his food, and moved his seat at home.
He did not tire of rice that was finely milled or meat that was finely minced. He did not eat rice that had gone sour or turned, fish that was spoiled, or meat that was rotten. He did not eat what was of bad colour or bad smell, what was badly cooked, or what was out of season. He did not eat meat that was not cut properly, or what lacked its proper sauce. However much meat there was, he did not let it outweigh the rice. Only with wine had he no fixed limit, but he never reached confusion. He did not eat wine or dried meat bought from the market. He did not take the ginger away at the end of a meal. He did not eat too much.
When he assisted at the ruler's sacrifice, he did not keep the meat overnight. Sacrificial meat at home was not kept beyond three days; after three days it was not eaten.
At meals he did not talk; in bed he did not speak. Even with coarse rice, vegetable soup or melon, he always made an offering, and always with solemnity.
If his mat was not straight, he did not sit on it.
When the villagers drank wine together, he left after those with walking sticks had gone out. When the villagers held the exorcism, he put on court dress and stood on the eastern steps.
When he sent a message of greeting to a person in another state, he bowed twice as he saw the messenger off. When Ji Kang sent him medicine, he bowed and accepted it, saying: "I do not know it, so I dare not taste it."
When the stables burned down, the Master came back from court and said: "Was anyone hurt?" He did not ask about the horses.
When the ruler sent him cooked food, he always straightened his mat and tasted it first. When the ruler sent raw meat, he always cooked it and offered it to his ancestors. When the ruler sent a live animal, he always kept it alive. When he dined in attendance on the ruler and the ruler made the offering, he tasted the food first.
When he was ill and the ruler came to see him, he lay with his head to the east, laid his court robe over himself and drew his sash across. When the ruler's command summoned him, he set out on foot without waiting for his carriage to be harnessed.
On entering the Grand Temple, he asked about everything.
When a friend died and had no one to take charge, he said: "I shall see to the funeral." When a friend sent a gift, even carriages and horses, he did not bow unless it was sacrificial meat.
In bed he did not lie like a corpse; at home he did not put on a formal manner.
When he saw someone in mourning dress, even a close friend, his expression changed. When he saw someone in ceremonial cap, or a blind person, even in private he was always courteous. When he met someone in mourning clothes, he bowed forward with his hand on the carriage rail, and he did the same to someone carrying the state registers. At a lavish feast, he always changed his expression and rose to his feet. At a sudden clap of thunder or a violent wind, he always changed his expression.
When he got into a carriage, he stood upright and held the cord. In the carriage he did not look back, did not speak quickly and did not point.
Startled, the bird rises; it circles, and then settles. He said: "The hen pheasant on the mountain bridge - how timely! How timely!" Zilu made a gesture to it; it sniffed three times and flew up.

keyLines.line: 孔子於鄉黨，恂恂如也，似不能言者
keyLines.en: In his home village Confucius was gentle and deferential, like one who could not speak.
keyLines.note: In his village, Confucius was mild and respectful, as if unable to speak; in the ancestral temple and at court he spoke fully and clearly, only with care.

keyLines.line: 入公門，鞠躬如也，如不容
keyLines.en: Entering the gate of the duke's palace, he bowed, as if there were no room for him.
keyLines.note: On entering the palace gate he bent his body as if the doorway could not hold him, a sign of respect.

keyLines.line: 食不厭精，膾不厭細
keyLines.en: He did not tire of rice finely milled or meat finely minced.
keyLines.note: He was not tired of finely milled grain or finely cut meat. It is often misread as a love of luxury; the original sense is care and seriousness about food.

keyLines.line: 色惡不食，臭惡不食。失飪不食，不時不食
keyLines.en: He would not eat if the colour was bad, nor if the smell was bad. He would not eat what was badly cooked, nor what was out of season.
keyLines.note: He would not eat food that had a bad colour, a bad smell, was badly cooked, or was out of season.

keyLines.line: 唯酒無量，不及亂
keyLines.en: Only for wine there was no set limit, but he never reached the point of confusion.
keyLines.note: He set no limit on wine, but he did not drink to the point of being disorderly.

keyLines.line: 食不語，寢不言
keyLines.en: He did not speak at meals or in bed.
keyLines.note: He did not talk while eating or while lying down to sleep.

keyLines.line: 廄焚，子退朝，曰：「傷人乎？」不問馬
keyLines.en: When the stable burned down, the Master came back from court and said: 'Was anyone hurt?' He did not ask about the horses.
keyLines.note: When the stable caught fire, Confucius came back from court and asked only whether anyone had been hurt, not about the horses. It shows how much he valued people.

keyLines.line: 入太廟，每事問
keyLines.en: On entering the Grand Temple, he asked about everything.
keyLines.note: On entering the Grand Temple he asked about each thing, out of respect for ritual.

glossary.note: A home district. In the Zhou, five hundred families made a 「黨」, and twelve thousand five hundred a 「鄉」.
Mild and deferential.
A look of respect and unease.
A deep blue shading to red, close to black, used for fasting and mourning garments; it could not be used for the collar trim.

glossary.en: yi er ai - 'spoiled and gone off'
glossary.note: Food that has turned sour or changed in smell.
The same as 「軾」, the crossbar at the front of a carriage; to lean on it and bow was a way of paying respect.

pian10.background: This whole book describes Confucius's everyday words and deeds. Unlike most of the other books of the Analects, which are sayings, it is thought to be a detailed record by his disciples of how their teacher lived, and is also material for the study of ritual and daily life in the Spring and Autumn period.

pian11.summary: Book 11, 'Xian jin', records the four fields of Confucius's school, the death of Yan Yuan, and the scene in which Zilu and three others sit with the Master and tell their aims (of which Zeng Dian's best pleases him). It contains such famous sayings as 'not yet knowing life, how can we know death', 'to overshoot is the same as to fall short', and the teaching of each person according to his nature.
pian11.translation:
The Master said: "Those who came first to ritual and music were rustics; those who came later are noble persons. If I were to use them, I would follow those who came first."
The Master said: "Of those who followed me in Chen and Cai, none is now at my door."
Excellent in virtuous conduct: Yan Yuan, Min Ziqian, Ran Boniu, Zhonggong. In speech: Zai Wo, Zigong. In government affairs: Ran You, Jilu. In literature and learning: Ziyou, Zixia.
The Master said: "Hui is no help to me: he is pleased with everything I say."
The Master said: "How filial Min Ziqian is! No one finds fault with what his parents and brothers say of him."
Nan Rong repeated the poem 'The White Jade Sceptre' three times, and Confucius gave him his elder brother's daughter in marriage.
Ji Kangzi asked: "Which of your disciples is fond of learning?" Confucius replied: "There was Yan Hui, who was fond of learning. Unfortunately his life was short and he died. Now there is no one."
When Yan Yuan died, Yan Lu asked for the Master's carriage to make an outer coffin for him. The Master said: "Gifted or not, each of us speaks of his own son. When Li died, he had an inner coffin and no outer coffin. I did not go on foot in order to give him an outer coffin, for since I follow behind the grandees I may not go on foot."
When Yan Yuan died, the Master said: "Alas! Heaven has destroyed me! Heaven has destroyed me!"
When Yan Yuan died, the Master wept for him beyond restraint. His followers said: "Master, you are beyond restraint!" He said: "Am I? If not for this man, for whom would I be?"
When Yan Yuan died, the disciples wished to give him a lavish funeral. The Master said: "You must not." The disciples gave him a lavish funeral all the same. The Master said: "Hui treated me like a father, but I was not able to treat him like a son. That is not my doing; it is you, my friends."
Jilu asked about serving the spirits. The Master said: "You cannot yet serve people; how could you serve spirits?" "May I ask about death?" "You do not yet know life; how could you know death?"
Min Ziqian stood beside the Master, upright and respectful; Zilu, bold and strong; Ran You and Zigong, easy and frank. The Master was pleased. He said: "Someone like You will not die a natural death."
The people of Lu were rebuilding the Long Treasury. Min Ziqian said: "What about keeping to the old one? Why must it be rebuilt?" The Master said: "That man does not speak much, but when he speaks he hits the mark."
The Master said: "What is You's zither doing at my gate?" The disciples stopped respecting Zilu. The Master said: "You has come up into the hall; he has not yet entered the inner room."
Zigong asked: "Which is the better, Shi or Shang?" The Master said: "Shi goes too far; Shang does not go far enough." "Then is Shi better?" The Master said: "Going too far is just like not going far enough."
The Ji family was richer than the Duke of Zhou, and Qiu collected taxes for them and added to their wealth. The Master said: "He is no disciple of mine. My friends, you may beat the drum and attack him."
Chai is simple, Shen is slow, Shi is showy, You is rough.
The Master said: "Hui comes close, though he is often in want. Ci does not accept his lot; he deals in goods, and his guesses are often right."
Zizhang asked about the way of a good person. The Master said: "He does not follow in others' footprints, and he does not enter the inner room either."
The Master said: "When someone is praised for sincere speech, is he a noble person, or only someone who looks grave?"
Zilu asked: "When I hear something, should I act on it at once?" The Master said: "With your father and elder brothers alive, how can you act on it at once?" Ran You asked: "When I hear something, should I act on it at once?" The Master said: "Act on it at once." Gongxi Hua said: "When You asked, 'Should I act at once?', you said, 'Your father and brothers are alive.' When Qiu asked, 'Should I act at once?', you said, 'Act at once.' I am puzzled and venture to ask why." The Master said: "Qiu holds back, so I pushed him on. You takes on the work of two people, so I held him back."
The Master was held in fear at Kuang, and Yan Yuan fell behind. The Master said: "I thought you were dead." He said: "While you are alive, Master, how would Hui dare to die?"
Ji Ziran asked: "Can Zhong You and Ran Qiu be called great ministers?" The Master said: "I thought you were going to ask something out of the ordinary, and you ask about You and Qiu! What is called a great minister serves his lord by the Way, and when that is not possible, he stops. As for You and Qiu, they can be called ministers who fill a post." "Then would they simply follow orders?" The Master said: "They would not follow orders to kill their father or their ruler."
Zilu had Zigao made steward of Bi. The Master said: "You are ruining another man's son." Zilu said: "There are people there, and altars of the land and grain. Why must one read books before one counts as having learned?" The Master said: "This is why I dislike glib talkers."
Zilu, Zeng Xi, Ran You and Gongxi Hua were sitting with the Master. The Master said: "Do not hold back because I am a day or two older than you. You are always saying, 'No one understands me.' If someone did understand you, what would you do?"
Zilu answered at once: "Give me a state of a thousand chariots, hemmed in between great states, pressed by armies and followed by famine. In three years I could make its people brave and give them a sense of direction." The Master smiled at him.
"Qiu, what about you?" He answered: "A territory sixty or seventy li square, or fifty or sixty. In three years I could make its people prosperous. As for ritual and music, I would wait for a noble person to do that."
"Chi, what about you?" He answered: "I do not say I can do it, but I would like to learn. At the affairs of the ancestral temple, or at meetings of the lords, wearing the dark robe and the ceremonial cap, I would like to be a minor assistant."
"Dian, what about you?" He was strumming his zither slowly; it ended with a ring. He put the zither aside and rose, and answered: "My wish differs from the three others' choices." The Master said: "What harm is there? Each is just stating his aim." He said: "In late spring, when the spring clothes are ready, I would go with five or six young men and six or seven boys to bathe in the Yi river, take the breeze at the Rain Altar, and return home singing." The Master sighed deeply and said: "I am with Dian!"
The other three went out, and Zeng Xi stayed behind. Zeng Xi said: "What did you think of what the three said?" The Master said: "Each was just stating his aim." "Why did you smile at You?" "To govern a state requires ritual, and his words were not yielding. That is why I smiled." "Was Qiu not speaking of a state?" "Where do you see sixty or seventy li, or fifty or sixty, that is not a state?" "Was Chi not speaking of a state?" "Ancestral temple and meetings of the lords - what are these if not the affairs of the lords? If Chi is to be a minor assistant, who could be a major one?"

keyLines.line: 德行：顏淵、閔子騫、冉伯牛、仲弓。言語：宰我、子貢。政事：冉有、季路。文學：子游、子夏
keyLines.en: Virtue and conduct: Yan Yuan, Min Ziqian, Ran Boniu, Zhonggong. Speech: Zai Wo, Zigong. Government: Ran You, Jilu. Letters: Ziyou, Zixia.
keyLines.note: The four fields and ten sages of Confucius's school: virtue, speech, government and letters. It is the first form of the Confucian division of studies.

keyLines.line: 天喪予！天喪予
keyLines.en: Heaven has destroyed me! Heaven has destroyed me!
keyLines.note: When Yan Yuan died, Confucius cried out in grief that Heaven had destroyed him, showing his deep feeling for Yan Hui.

keyLines.line: 未能事人，焉能事鬼
keyLines.en: You cannot yet serve men; how can you serve the spirits?
keyLines.note: Zilu asked how to serve the spirits; Confucius replied that he cannot yet serve the living, so how could he serve the spirits? It shows the Confucian concern with human affairs.

keyLines.line: 未知生，焉知死
keyLines.en: You do not yet know life; how can you know death?
keyLines.note: Zilu then asked about death; Confucius answered that he did not yet understand life, so how could he understand death? He put the weight on actual human life.

keyLines.line: 過猶不及
keyLines.en: To overshoot is the same as to fall short.
keyLines.note: Zigong asked which was better, Shi (Zizhang) or Shang (Zixia). Confucius said Zizhang goes too far and Zixia not far enough, and the two are equally flawed. It is an important saying for the idea of the mean.

keyLines.line: 求也退，故進之；由也兼人，故退之
keyLines.en: Ran Qiu holds back, so I push him on; You has the energy of two men, so I hold him back.
keyLines.note: To the same question, 'should I act at once when I hear something?', Confucius told Ran You 'do it' and told Zilu 'you have your father and elder brother'. This was because Ran You is timid and Zilu is combative, so he taught each according to his nature.

keyLines.line: 莫春者，春服既成。冠者五六人，童子六七人。浴乎沂，風乎舞雩，詠而歸
keyLines.en: In late spring, when the spring clothes are ready, with five or six grown men and six or seven boys, I would bathe in the Yi, enjoy the breeze at the Wuyu altar, and return home singing.
keyLines.note: What Zeng Dian wished for: in late spring, dressed in spring clothes, with five or six men and six or seven boys, to bathe in the River Yi, enjoy the air at the Wuyu terrace, and come home singing.

keyLines.line: 吾與點也
keyLines.en: I am with Dian!
keyLines.note: Confucius sighed that he approved of Zeng Dian, because his wish showed a harmony of man and Heaven and a delight in a natural life.

glossary.en: xian jin, hou jin - 'earlier and later advancers'
glossary.note: One reading takes them as the older and younger generations; another takes them as the country folk who learned ritual and music first and the gentlemen who learned later.

glossary.en: bu ji men - 'not at my door'
glossary.note: No longer in Confucius's school, meaning no longer by his side at the time.
The outer coffin that encloses the inner one.
Hasty and blunt.
To smile.
The altar in Lu for sacrifices to Heaven and for praying for rain, beside the Yi river.

pian11.background: This book discusses Confucius's disciples and their aims, and is among the most vivid in the Analects in the portrayal of people. The 'sitting in attendance' passage runs to over four hundred characters and is a main basis for later readings of Confucius's ideal world.

pian12.summary: Book 12, 'Yan Yuan', is wholly about humaneness, government and the noble person. To overcome oneself and return to ritual is humaneness; do not look, listen, speak or act against ritual; what you do not want, do not do to others. In government, there must be enough food, arms and trust, and the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister; the wind over the grass bends it. It also treats distinguishing delusion and the difference between 'being known' and 'being renowned'.
pian12.translation:
Yan Yuan asked about humaneness. The Master said: "To overcome the self and return to ritual is humaneness. If for a single day one overcame the self and returned to ritual, the whole world would turn to humaneness. Humaneness comes from oneself - does it come from others?" Yan Yuan said: "May I ask for the details?" The Master said: "Do not look at what is contrary to ritual; do not listen to what is contrary to ritual; do not speak what is contrary to ritual; do not move contrary to ritual." Yan Yuan said: "Though I am not quick, I ask to put these words into practice."
Zhonggong asked about humaneness. The Master said: "When you go out of your door, behave as if you were meeting an honoured guest. Employ the people as if you were assisting at a great sacrifice. What you do not want for yourself, do not impose on others. Then there will be no resentment against you in the state, and no resentment in the family." Zhonggong said: "Though I am not quick, I ask to put these words into practice."
Sima Niu asked about humaneness. The Master said: "The humane person is slow to speak." "Slow to speak - is that what is called humaneness?" The Master said: "It is hard to do; how could one not be slow to speak of it?"
Sima Niu asked about the noble person. The Master said: "The noble person is free of worry and fear." "Free of worry and fear - is that what is called a noble person?" The Master said: "If on looking within he finds nothing to be ashamed of, what is there to worry about or fear?"
Sima Niu said sadly: "Everyone has brothers; I alone have none." Zixia said: "I have heard it said: 'Life and death are fated; wealth and rank rest with Heaven.' A noble person is reverent and makes no mistakes, and is courteous and observes ritual with others; then all within the four seas are his brothers. Why should a noble person worry about having no brothers?"
Zizhang asked about clear-sightedness. The Master said: "If slander that seeps in like water, and accusations that bite into the skin, do not work on someone, he can be called clear-sighted. If they do not work on him, he can be called far-sighted too."
Zigong asked about government. The Master said: "Enough food, enough weapons, and the trust of the people." Zigong said: "If one had to give up one of these, which should go first?" "The weapons." Zigong said: "If one had to give up one of the remaining two, which should go first?" "The food. Since ancient times everyone has died, but a people without trust cannot stand."
Ji Zicheng said: "A noble person is simply substance. What need has he of refinement?" Zigong said: "What a pity, Sir, that you speak of the noble person like that! Four horses cannot catch up with the tongue. Refinement is like substance, and substance is like refinement. The hide of a tiger or leopard, once the hair is removed, is like the hide of a dog or sheep."
Duke Ai asked You Ruo: "It is a year of famine and there is not enough for expenses. What should I do?" You Ruo replied: "Why not use the tithe of one tenth?" The Duke said: "Two tenths is not enough for me. How could I use one tenth?" He replied: "If the people have enough, with whom could the ruler not have enough? If the people do not have enough, with whom could the ruler have enough?"
Zizhang asked how to raise virtue and see through confusion. The Master said: "Take loyalty and trustworthiness as your chief principles and move towards what is right: this is raising virtue. When you love someone you want him to live; when you hate someone you want him to die. To want him to live and then to want him to die - this is confusion. 'Truly, not for the sake of wealth, but only for the sake of novelty.'"
Duke Jing of Qi asked Confucius about government. Confucius replied: "Let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son." The Duke said: "Well said! If the ruler is not a ruler, the minister not a minister, the father not a father, the son not a son, then even if there is grain, could I get to eat it?"
The Master said: "Someone who can settle a lawsuit with half a word - that would be You." Zilu never let a promise stand overnight.
The Master said: "In hearing lawsuits, I am like anyone else. What we must do is make sure there are no lawsuits."
Zizhang asked about government. The Master said: "Hold the post without growing weary, and carry out the work with loyalty."
The Master said: "The noble person who studies widely in literature and keeps himself in check with ritual will not go astray."
The Master said: "The noble person helps others achieve what is good and does not help them achieve what is bad. The petty person is the opposite."
Ji Kangzi asked Confucius about government. Confucius replied: "To govern (zheng) is to be correct (zheng). If you lead by being correct, who will dare not to be correct?"
Ji Kangzi was troubled by thieves and asked Confucius. Confucius replied: "If you yourself did not desire wealth, they would not steal even if you rewarded them."
Ji Kangzi asked Confucius about government: "What if I killed those who lack the Way, so as to bring the Way to those who have it?" Confucius replied: "In governing, what need is there to kill? If you desire the good, the people will be good. The virtue of the noble person is the wind; the virtue of the petty person is the grass. When the wind blows over the grass, it must bend."
Zizhang asked: "What must a scholar be like to be called 'successful'?" The Master said: "What do you mean by 'successful'?" Zizhang replied: "To be known in the state and known in the family." The Master said: "That is 'being known', not 'being successful'. Someone who is successful is straight by nature and loves what is right; he reads people's words and watches their expressions, and thinks to put himself below others. He is sure to succeed in the state and sure to succeed in the family. Someone who is 'known' puts on a humane look while his conduct goes against it, and has no doubts about himself. He is sure to be known in the state and sure to be known in the family."
Fan Chi was walking with the Master below the Rain Altar and said: "May I ask how to raise virtue, root out hidden evil, and see through confusion?" The Master said: "A good question! To put the work first and the reward after - is that not raising virtue? To attack your own evil and not attack the evil of others - is that not rooting out hidden evil? To forget yourself and endanger your parents in a fit of morning anger - is that not confusion?"
Fan Chi asked about humaneness. The Master said: "Love people." He asked about wisdom. The Master said: "Know people." Fan Chi did not understand. The Master said: "Raise up the upright and set them over the crooked, and you can make the crooked straight." Fan Chi withdrew and saw Zixia, and said: "A moment ago I saw the Master and asked about wisdom. The Master said, 'Raise up the upright and set them over the crooked, and you can make the crooked straight.' What did he mean?" Zixia said: "How rich those words are! When Shun held the world, he chose from the multitude and raised up Gao Yao, and the inhumane stayed far away. When Tang held the world, he chose from the multitude and raised up Yi Yin, and the inhumane stayed far away."
Zigong asked about friends. The Master said: "Advise them loyally and guide them well. If they will not listen, stop. Do not bring disgrace on yourself."
Master Zeng said: "The noble person gathers friends through culture, and through friends supports humaneness."

keyLines.line: 克己復禮為仁。一日克己復禮，天下歸仁焉
keyLines.en: To overcome oneself and return to ritual is humaneness. If for one day one overcomes oneself and returns to ritual, the whole world will turn to humaneness.
keyLines.note: To restrain oneself so that words and deeds accord with ritual is humaneness; if one managed it for a single day, all the world would call him humane. There are many readings of 'overcome oneself'; Zhu Xi took it as overcoming selfish desire.

keyLines.line: 非禮勿視，非禮勿聽，非禮勿言，非禮勿動
keyLines.en: Do not look at what is against ritual, do not listen to what is against ritual, do not speak what is against ritual, do not do what is against ritual.
keyLines.note: The answer to Yan Yuan's question about the items of humaneness: do not look, listen, speak or act contrary to ritual.

keyLines.line: 出門如見大賓，使民如承大祭，己所不欲，勿施於人
keyLines.en: When you go out, behave as if receiving an honoured guest; employ the people as if conducting a great sacrifice; what you do not want yourself, do not do to others.
keyLines.note: The answer to Zhonggong on humaneness: outside the door, act as if meeting a distinguished guest; in employing the people, act as though presiding over a great sacrifice; and do not do to others what you do not want.

keyLines.line: 內省不疚，夫何憂何懼
keyLines.en: If on looking inward there is nothing to be ashamed of, what is there to worry about or fear?
keyLines.note: The answer to Sima Niu on the noble person: if on examining himself he finds no fault, what has he to worry or fear?

keyLines.line: 死生有命，富貴在天
keyLines.en: Life and death are a matter of fate; wealth and rank are with Heaven.
keyLines.note: Zixia's words to comfort Sima Niu: life and death are fate and wealth and rank are Heaven's; if the noble person is careful, faultless, respectful and polite, then all within the four seas are his brothers.

keyLines.line: 去食。自古皆有死，民無信不立
keyLines.en: Give up the food. Since ancient times all men have died, but without the trust of the people a state cannot stand.
keyLines.note: Zigong asked about government. If one of three (food, arms, trust) must go, drop arms first, then food, but keep trust at the last. If the people do not trust the government, the state cannot stand.

keyLines.line: 君君，臣臣，父父，子子
keyLines.en: Let the ruler be a ruler, the minister a minister, the father a father, the son a son.
keyLines.note: Reply to Duke Jing of Qi on government: the ruler should act as a ruler, the minister as a minister, and so with father and son: each fulfilling his role.

keyLines.line: 子欲善，而民善矣。君子之德，風；小人之德，草；草上之風，必偃
keyLines.en: If you want to be good, the people will be good. The virtue of the noble person is like the wind; the virtue of the petty person is like grass; the grass, when the wind blows over it, must bend.
keyLines.note: If the ruler himself wants goodness, the people will follow; the virtue of the noble is like the wind and that of the petty like grass, and when the wind blows the grass bends.

glossary.en: ke ji fu li - 'to overcome oneself and return to ritual'
glossary.note: 「克己」 is to restrain oneself and 「復禮」 is to return to the norms of ritual.
Slow and careful of speech.

glossary.en: jin run zhi zen, fu shou zhi su - 'seeping slander, slander that cuts the skin'
glossary.note: Slander that soaks in like water, and accusations that hurt as close as one's own skin.

glossary.en: si bu ji she - 'four horses cannot overtake the tongue'
glossary.note: Once a word is out, even a carriage and four cannot catch it.
The Zhou tax of one tenth.

glossary.en: da yu wen - 'to be accomplished and to be renowned'
glossary.note: 「達」 is to be accomplished in virtue and 「聞」 is to have an empty name.

pian12.background: This book is regarded as the one that discusses humaneness most intensively in the Analects. Confucius gives humaneness different answers for different disciples, which shows his habit of teaching each according to his nature.

pian13.summary: Book 13, 'Zilu', covers the way of governing: set the example and make the people work, rectify names, make them numerous, then enrich them, then teach them, and set oneself right. It also touches on how noble and petty persons get along, uprightness within the family, the wild and the cautious versus the middle way, and the ranks of the scholar.
pian13.translation:
Zilu asked about government. The Master said: "Go ahead of the people; put them to work." He asked for more. "Do not grow weary."
Zhonggong was steward of the Ji family and asked about government. The Master said: "Give first place to your officials. Forgive small faults. Promote the worthy and talented." He asked: "How do I recognise the worthy and talented in order to promote them?" The Master said: "Promote those you know. As for those you do not know, will others pass them over?"
Zilu said: "The ruler of Wei is waiting for you to govern. What will you do first?" The Master said: "It must be to rectify names." Zilu said: "Is that so? How impractical you are, Master! What is there to rectify?" The Master said: "How crude you are, You! A noble person holds back where he does not understand. If names are not correct, speech does not follow; if speech does not follow, affairs are not accomplished; if affairs are not accomplished, ritual and music do not flourish; if ritual and music do not flourish, punishments miss their mark; if punishments miss their mark, the people do not know where to put hand or foot. So a noble person must be able to speak what he names, and what he speaks he must be able to carry out. In his words, a noble person is never careless."
Fan Chi asked to learn farming. The Master said: "I am not as good as an old farmer." He asked to learn gardening. "I am not as good as an old gardener." When Fan Chi had gone out, the Master said: "What a petty man Fan Xu is! If those above love ritual, the people will not dare not to be respectful. If those above love what is right, the people will not dare not to obey. If those above love trustworthiness, the people will not dare not to be sincere. If it is so, people from all quarters will come with their children on their backs. What need is there to farm?"
The Master said: "A man may recite the three hundred Songs, yet when given a post in government he cannot manage it, or sent on a mission to other states he cannot reply on his own. However many he has learned, what use are they?"
The Master said: "If he is correct himself, orders are carried out without being given. If he is not correct himself, they are not followed even when given."
The Master said: "The governments of Lu and Wei are brothers."
The Master said of Prince Jing of Wei: "He ran his household well. When he first had something, he said, 'It will do.' When he had a little more, he said, 'It is quite complete.' When he had plenty, he said, 'It is quite fine.'"
The Master went to Wei, and Ran You drove his carriage. The Master said: "How populous!" Ran You said: "When they are populous, what more can be done?" "Make them rich." "When they are rich, what more can be done?" "Teach them."
The Master said: "If anyone would employ me, in a year I could do something, and in three years I would have results."
The Master said: "'If good people ruled a state for a hundred years, they could overcome cruelty and do away with killing.' How true this saying is!"
The Master said: "If a true king arose, it would still take a generation for humaneness to prevail."
The Master said: "If you can set yourself right, what difficulty is there in government? If you cannot set yourself right, how can you set others right?"
Ran Zi came back from court. The Master said: "Why so late?" He replied: "There was government business." The Master said: "Ordinary business, surely! If there had been government business, I would have heard of it, even though I am not employed."
Duke Ding asked: "Is it true that a single saying can make a state flourish?" Confucius replied: "A saying cannot be expected to do that. People say: 'It is hard to be a ruler; being a minister is not easy either.' If a ruler knows how hard it is to be a ruler, is that not close to a single saying making a state flourish?" "Is it true that a single saying can ruin a state?" Confucius replied: "A saying cannot be expected to do that. People say: 'I take no pleasure in being a ruler, except that no one opposes what I say.' If what he says is good and no one opposes it, that is good. But if what he says is not good and no one opposes it, is that not close to a single saying ruining a state?"
The Lord of She asked about government. The Master said: "Make those near happy, and those far will come."
Zixia was steward of Jufu and asked about government. The Master said: "Do not want speed; do not look at small gains. If you want speed you will not arrive; if you look at small gains, the great things will not be done."
The Lord of She told Confucius: "In my district there is a man called Upright Gong. When his father stole a sheep, he gave evidence against him." Confucius said: "The upright people in my district are different. A father covers for his son, and a son covers for his father. Uprightness is found in that."
Fan Chi asked about humaneness. The Master said: "At home, be respectful; in your work, be reverent; with others, be loyal. Even if you go among the barbarians, you must not give these up."
Zigong asked: "What must a person be like to be called a scholar-official?" The Master said: "One who has a sense of shame in his conduct and, sent on a mission to other states, does not disgrace his ruler's commission can be called a scholar-official." "May I ask the next level?" "One whom his clan calls filial and whom his village calls respectful of elders." "May I ask the next?" "One whose word is always true and whose actions always carry through - stubborn and small-minded as he is, he may count as the next level." "What about those who hold office today?" The Master said: "Ah! Those narrow vessels, hardly worth counting!"
The Master said: "If I cannot find people who follow the middle way to teach, I would take the wild and the cautious. The wild push forward; the cautious will not do certain things."
The Master said: "The people of the south have a saying: 'A man without constancy cannot be a shaman or a healer.' How good! 'If he is not constant in his virtue, he may bring himself shame.'" The Master said: "It is simply that he need not consult the oracle."
The Master said: "The noble person is harmonious but not uniform; the petty person is uniform but not harmonious."
Zigong asked: "What if everyone in the village likes him?" The Master said: "That is not enough." "What if everyone in the village dislikes him?" The Master said: "That is not enough. Better that the good people in the village like him and the bad ones dislike him."
The Master said: "A noble person is easy to serve and hard to please. If you please him by wrong means, he is not pleased; and when he employs people, he uses them according to their abilities. A petty person is hard to serve and easy to please. If you please him by wrong means, he is pleased; and when he employs people, he demands that they be perfect."
The Master said: "The noble person is at ease without being proud; the petty person is proud without being at ease."
The Master said: "Firm, resolute, plain and slow of speech - these are close to humaneness."
Zilu asked: "What must a person be like to be called a scholar-official?" The Master said: "Earnest, encouraging, and cheerful - such a person can be called a scholar-official: earnest and encouraging with friends, cheerful with brothers."
The Master said: "If good people taught the people for seven years, they could be sent to war."
The Master said: "To send the people to war without teaching them is to throw them away."

keyLines.line: 先之，勞之
keyLines.en: Set the example, and make them work.
keyLines.note: Zilu asked about government. Confucius replied: lead the way yourself and make the people work hard. Asked for more, he said: 'do not tire'.

keyLines.line: 必也正名乎
keyLines.en: What is necessary is the rectification of names!
keyLines.note: The ruler of Wei was waiting for Confucius to take office, and Confucius's first step would be to 'rectify names', making titles match reality.

keyLines.line: 名不正，則言不順；言不順，則事不成
keyLines.en: If names are not rectified, speech does not follow; if speech does not follow, affairs are not accomplished.
keyLines.note: The chain of reasoning for rectifying names: wrong names, speech does not follow, affairs fail, ritual and music do not flourish, punishments miss the mark, and the people do not know where to put hand or foot.

keyLines.line: 其身正，不令而行；其身不正，雖令不從
keyLines.en: If a ruler is himself upright, his orders are carried out without being given; if he is not upright, even though he gives orders, they will not be followed.
keyLines.note: If those who govern are themselves upright, things are done without orders; if they are not, orders are not obeyed.

keyLines.line: 庶矣哉
keyLines.en: What a multitude!
keyLines.note: On arriving in Wei, Confucius sighed at the number of people. Ran You asked what should be added; he said 'enrich them'. Asked again, he said 'teach them'.

keyLines.line: 無欲速，無見小利。欲速，則不達；見小利，則大事不成
keyLines.en: Do not be in a hurry, and do not look at small gains. If you are in a hurry, you do not get there; if you look at small gains, great things are not accomplished.
keyLines.note: Reply to Zixia on government: do not seek speed or small profit; haste does not arrive and petty gain spoils great undertakings.

keyLines.line: 父為子隱，子為父隱，直在其中矣
keyLines.en: The father covers up for the son, and the son covers up for the father; uprightness lies in that.
keyLines.note: Reply to the Duke of She: the upright in my part of the country are different from this: the father hides for the son and the son for the father, and uprightness is in that. It reflects the Confucian regard for family feeling.

keyLines.line: 君子和而不同，小人同而不和
keyLines.en: The noble person is in harmony but does not conform; the petty person conforms but is not in harmony.
keyLines.note: The noble person gets along without simply agreeing; the petty person agrees blindly but cannot be in harmony.

glossary.note: To make titles and designations match reality and so fix ethical roles.
To leave in doubt, to not speak rashly.

glossary.en: qiang fu - 'to carry on the back'
glossary.note: To carry a baby on the back in a cloth sling.

glossary.en: kuang juan - 'the wild and the cautious'
glossary.note: The wild go forward boldly; the cautious keep themselves clean and refuse to act.

glossary.en: dou shao zhi ren - 'a measure-and-basket man'
glossary.note: A person of small capacity. A 「斗」 and a 「筲」 are small vessels.
Rigid and obstinate.

pian13.background: The passage on 'rectifying names' is often used to discuss Confucius's political thought, and the one on a father covering up for his son has stirred long discussion about family feeling against public justice.

pian14.summary: Book 14, 'Xian wen', opens with Xian (Yuan Xian) asking about shame, and ranges over the scholar, humaneness, the complete man and the noble person, with comments on Guan Zhong, Zichan and others. It gives 'repay uprightness for resentment', 'study below and reach above' and 'in ancient times men studied for themselves'.
pian14.translation:
Xian asked about shame. The Master said: "When the state has the Way, to draw a salary; when the state lacks the Way, to draw a salary - that is shame."
"If one does not act from overbearing, boasting, resentment or greed, can that be called humaneness?" The Master said: "It can be called difficult, but whether it is humaneness I do not know."
The Master said: "A scholar who cherishes comfort at home is not fit to be a scholar."
The Master said: "When the state has the Way, speak boldly and act boldly. When the state lacks the Way, act boldly but speak with deference."
The Master said: "Those who have virtue are sure to have words, but those who have words do not always have virtue. The humane are sure to have courage, but the courageous are not always humane."
Nangong Kuo asked Confucius: "Yi was a fine archer and Ao could push a boat over dry land, yet neither died a natural death. Yu and Ji worked the land themselves and came to possess the world." The Master did not answer. When Nangong Kuo had gone out, the Master said: "What a noble person he is! How he honours virtue!"
The Master said: "There are noble persons who are not humane, but there has never been a petty person who is humane."
The Master said: "If you love someone, can you fail to make him work hard? If you are loyal to someone, can you fail to teach him?"
The Master said: "In drafting a diplomatic document, Pi Chen made the first draft, Shi Shu discussed it, the envoy Ziyu revised it, and Zichan of Dongli gave it its polish."
Someone asked about Zichan. The Master said: "He was a generous man." He asked about Zixi. "That man! That man!" He asked about Guan Zhong. "He was a man who took from the Bo family the three hundred households of Pian, and Bo ate coarse rice to the end of his life without a word of complaint."
The Master said: "To be poor without resentment is hard; to be rich without arrogance is easy."
The Master said: "Meng Gongchuo would be excellent as senior steward for the Zhao or Wei families, but he could not be a grandee of Teng or Xue."
Zilu asked about the complete person. The Master said: "With the wisdom of Zang Wuzhong, the freedom from desire of Gongchuo, the courage of Zhuangzi of Bian, the skills of Ran Qiu, refined by ritual and music, one could be called a complete person." He added: "But must the complete person of today be like that? One who, seeing profit, thinks of what is right; seeing danger, is ready to give his life; and does not forget the promises of a lifetime, even when it has been long - he too can be called a complete person."
The Master asked Gongming Jia about Gongshu Wenzi: "Is it true that your master does not speak, does not laugh, and does not take anything?" Gongming Jia replied: "Whoever told you that went too far. My master speaks only when the time is right, so people do not tire of his words. He laughs only when he is happy, so people do not tire of his laughter. He takes only what is right, so people do not tire of his taking." The Master said: "Is that so? Can that really be so?"
The Master said: "Zang Wuzhong used his city of Fang to demand a successor for his family in Lu. Though people say he was not forcing the ruler, I do not believe it."
The Master said: "Duke Wen of Jin was crafty and not upright; Duke Huan of Qi was upright and not crafty."
Zilu said: "When Duke Huan killed Prince Jiu, Shao Hu died for him, but Guan Zhong did not die. Was he not inhumane?" The Master said: "Duke Huan gathered the lords nine times without using war chariots; this was Guan Zhong's doing. Such was his humaneness! Such was his humaneness!"
Zigong said: "Was Guan Zhong not inhumane? When Duke Huan killed Prince Jiu, he could not die for him, and he even served as Huan's chief minister." The Master said: "Guan Zhong served as Duke Huan's chief minister, made him leader of the lords, and set the whole world right. To this day the people receive the benefit. Without Guan Zhong, we would be wearing our hair loose and fastening our robes on the left. Would he rather be faithful like an ordinary man or woman, who hangs himself in a ditch with no one the wiser?"
Gongshu Wenzi's retainer Zhuan was raised to the same rank as Wenzi in the ducal court. The Master heard of this and said: "He deserves the title 'Wen' (cultured)."
The Master spoke of Duke Ling of Wei's lack of the Way. Ji Kangzi said: "If that is so, why has he not lost his state?" Confucius said: "Zhongshu Yu manages guests, Priest Tuo manages the ancestral temple, and Wangsun Jia manages the army. With such men, how could he lose it?"
The Master said: "One who feels no shame in boasting will find it hard to live up to it."
Chen Chengzi killed Duke Jian. Confucius bathed, went to court, and reported to Duke Ai: "Chen Heng has killed his ruler. I request that he be punished." The Duke said: "Tell the three lords." Confucius said: "Because I follow behind the grandees, I did not dare not to report. And the ruler says, 'Tell the three lords'!" He went to the three lords and told them, and they would not consent. Confucius said: "Because I follow behind the grandees, I did not dare not to report."
Zilu asked about serving a ruler. The Master said: "Do not deceive him; and stand up to him."
The Master said: "The noble person goes up; the petty person goes down."
The Master said: "In ancient times people studied for themselves; nowadays people study for others."
Qu Boyu sent a messenger to Confucius. Confucius sat with him and asked: "What is your master doing?" He replied: "My master wishes to reduce his faults but has not yet managed to." The messenger went out. The Master said: "What a messenger! What a messenger!"
The Master said: "If you do not hold the position, do not plan its policy."
Master Zeng said: "The noble person's thoughts do not go beyond his position."
The Master said: "A noble person is ashamed when his words go beyond his deeds."
The Master said: "The noble person's way has three parts, and I have not achieved any of them: the humane do not worry, the wise are not confused, the brave are not afraid." Zigong said: "That is the Master describing himself."
Zigong was comparing people. The Master said: "Ci, are you so worthy? I have no time for that."
The Master said: "Do not worry that others do not know you; worry that you lack ability."
The Master said: "One who does not expect deceit and does not assume bad faith, yet is among the first to notice it - is he not worthy?"
Weisheng Mu said to Confucius: "Qiu, why do you keep going about from place to place? Are you not just being glib?" Confucius said: "I do not dare to be glib; I hate stubbornness."
The Master said: "A fine horse is not praised for its strength but for its character."
Someone said: "What about repaying resentment with virtue?" The Master said: "Then with what will you repay virtue? Repay resentment with justice, and repay virtue with virtue."
The Master said: "No one knows me!" Zigong said: "Why does no one know you?" The Master said: "I do not complain against Heaven or blame people. I learn from the lowly and reach up to the heights. The one who knows me is Heaven."
Gongbo Liao slandered Zilu to Ji Sun. Zifu Jingbo reported it, saying: "The Master has certainly been misled by Gongbo Liao, but I still have the power to have him exposed in the market-place." The Master said: "If the Way is to prevail, it is fate; if the Way is to fail, it is fate. What can Gongbo Liao do against fate?"
The Master said: "The worthy withdraw from the world; the next withdraw from a place; the next withdraw from a rude look; the next withdraw from harsh words."
The Master said: "Seven men have done so."
Zilu spent the night at Stone Gate. The gatekeeper said: "Where are you from?" Zilu said: "From the house of Confucius." He said: "Is that the one who knows it cannot be done and does it anyway?"
The Master was striking the chime stone in Wei. A man carrying a basket passed the gate of the Master's house and said: "Someone with a heart is striking the stone!" After a while he said: "How coarse, that stubborn clang! If no one knows you, then just stop. 'If the water is deep, wade across in your clothes; if shallow, lift up your robes.'" The Master said: "How resolute! Then there is nothing hard about it."
Zizhang said: "The Book of Documents says: 'Gaozong stayed in the mourning hut for three years and did not speak.' What does it mean?" The Master said: "Why Gaozong only? All people in ancient times did so. When a ruler died, the hundred officials each did their own duties and took orders from the prime minister, for three years."
The Master said: "If those above love ritual, the people are easy to employ."
Zilu asked about the noble person. The Master said: "Cultivate yourself in reverence." "Is that all?" "Cultivate yourself so as to bring peace to others." "Is that all?" "Cultivate yourself so as to bring peace to all the people. Even Yao and Shun would have found it hard to fully achieve cultivating oneself so as to bring peace to all the people."
Yuan Rang squatted waiting for the Master. The Master said: "As a child you were not respectful, as an adult you have achieved nothing, and now you are old and will not die - you are a pest." And he struck his shin with his staff.
A boy from Que village was carrying messages. Someone asked: "Is he making progress?" The Master said: "I saw him sitting in the adults' seat, and walking side by side with his elders. He is not one who seeks progress; he wants quick results."

keyLines.line: 邦有道，穀；邦無道，穀，恥也
keyLines.en: When the state follows the Way, to draw a salary; when the state does not follow the Way, to draw a salary: that is shameful.
keyLines.note: The answer to Yuan Xian's question about shame: to draw pay in a well-governed state is right, but to draw pay and do nothing in a badly governed one is shameful.

keyLines.line: 克、伐、怨、欲，不行焉，可以為仁矣
keyLines.en: To have overcome love of victory, boasting, resentment and desire: may that be counted as humaneness?
keyLines.note: Xian asked whether it was humaneness to overcome love of winning, boasting, resentment and greed. Confucius said it is hard to do, but he did not know whether it is humaneness.

keyLines.line: 見利思義，見危授命，久要不忘平生之言，亦可以為成人矣
keyLines.en: One who thinks of rightness when he sees gain, risks his life when he sees danger, and does not forget the promises of a lifetime when long in want, may be called a complete man.
keyLines.note: Reply to Zilu on the 'complete man': thinks of rightness when he sees profit, gives his life in danger, and does not forget his old promises after long hardship.

keyLines.line: 管仲相桓公，霸諸侯，一匡天下，民到于今受其賜
keyLines.en: Guan Zhong helped Duke Huan, made him leader of the lords, and set the world right in one stroke; to this day the people receive his gifts.
keyLines.note: In defence of Guan Zhong: he helped Duke Huan of Qi to supremacy and set the world right, and the people still benefit; he should not be blamed for not dying for Prince Jiu.

keyLines.line: 或曰：「以德報怨，何如？」
keyLines.en: Someone said: 'What of repaying injury with kindness?'
keyLines.note: Someone asked about repaying resentment with kindness. Confucius asked in return: 'then with what do you repay kindness?' and answered: 'repay resentment with uprightness, and repay kindness with kindness'.

keyLines.line: 古之學者為己，今之學者為人
keyLines.en: In ancient times men studied for themselves; nowadays they study for others.
keyLines.note: In the past, people learned to improve themselves; now they learn to be seen by others, or to please them.

keyLines.line: 不怨天，不尤人，下學而上達，知我者，其天乎
keyLines.en: I do not complain against Heaven, nor blame men; I study below and reach above. The one who knows me, is it not Heaven?
keyLines.note: Confucius on himself: he does not grumble at Heaven or blame others, but by learning ordinary things reaches the mandate of Heaven; perhaps only Heaven understands him.

keyLines.line: 知其不可而為之者
keyLines.en: The one who knows it cannot be done and yet does it.
keyLines.note: The gatekeeper's comment on Confucius: 'the one who knows it is impossible and still does it'. It later came to sum up Confucius's active engagement with the world and loyalty to his ideals.

glossary.note: Yuan Xian, a disciple of Confucius.
The same as 「遜」: modest.
A perfect person with both virtue and ability.

glossary.en: jiu he zhu hou - 'nine assemblies of the lords'
glossary.note: Duke Huan of Qi called the lords to meetings many times; another view takes 'nine' as a figure for 'many'.

glossary.en: bei fa zuo ren - 'hair loose and robe fastened on the left'
glossary.note: The hair worn down and the front of the robe opening to the left: the dress and custom of the barbarians.
The sound of a stone chime that rings hard; a figure for obstinacy.

pian14.background: This book covers a wide range of topics. The phrase 'repay resentment with uprightness' contrasts with the Laozi's 'repay resentment with virtue', and is important material for comparing Confucian and Daoist attitudes. 'Uprightness' means dealing with it fairly and reasonably, neither returning grievance for grievance nor repaying with kindness without principle.

pian15.summary: Book 15, 'Wei Ling Gong', treats the way of the noble person: to bear poverty firmly, to link everything together with one thread, to govern by non-action, and to speak loyally and act with sincere reverence. It also covers giving up life to complete humaneness, 'a craftsman must first sharpen his tools', 'without far thought there is near worry', reciprocity as the one word to practise for a lifetime, teaching without distinction, and 'those on different paths do not plan together'.
pian15.translation:
Duke Ling of Wei asked Confucius about battle formations. Confucius replied: "I have heard about sacrificial vessels, but I have not studied military matters." The next day he left. In Chen the food ran out. His followers were so ill that none could stand. Zilu, angry, came to see him and said: "Does the noble person also come to hardship?" The Master said: "The noble person holds firm in hardship; the petty person in hardship runs wild."
The Master said: "Ci, do you think that I learn many things and remember them?" He answered: "Yes. Is it not so?" "No. I thread them together with one thing."
The Master said: "You, those who understand virtue are few."
The Master said: "One who ruled by doing nothing - that would be Shun, would it not? What did he do? He simply made himself reverent and sat facing south."
Zizhang asked how to get on in the world. The Master said: "If your words are loyal and trustworthy and your actions sincere and respectful, you will get on even among barbarian tribes. If your words are not loyal and trustworthy and your actions not sincere and respectful, will you get on even in your own village? When standing, see these before you; when in a carriage, see them resting on the yoke. Only then will you get on." Zizhang wrote it on his sash.
The Master said: "How straight was Shi Yu! When the state had the Way, he was like an arrow; when the state lacked the Way, he was like an arrow. What a noble person Qu Boyu was! When the state had the Way, he took office; when the state lacked the Way, he could roll himself up and tuck himself away."
The Master said: "If someone can be spoken with and you do not speak with him, you waste a person. If someone cannot be spoken with and you speak with him, you waste your words. The wise waste neither people nor words."
The Master said: "A man of purpose and a humane man will not seek life at the expense of humaneness; some will give up their lives to accomplish humaneness."
Zigong asked how to practise humaneness. The Master said: "A craftsman who wants to do his work well must first sharpen his tools. Living in a state, serve the worthy among its grandees and make friends with the humane among its scholars."
Yan Yuan asked about governing a state. The Master said: "Follow the calendar of the Xia, ride in the state carriage of the Yin, wear the ceremonial cap of the Zhou, and for music use the Shao and the Wu dances. Ban the songs of Zheng and keep glib people at a distance. The songs of Zheng are licentious, and glib people are dangerous."
The Master said: "One who has no far-sighted thought is sure to have trouble close at hand."
The Master said: "It is over! I have never seen anyone who loves virtue as much as he loves beauty."
The Master said: "Zang Wenzhong was one who held his post by theft, was he not? He knew Liuxia Hui was worthy, and did not help him to a place beside him."
The Master said: "Demand much of yourself and little of others, and you keep resentment at a distance."
The Master said: "If someone does not keep asking 'What should I do? What should I do?', there is nothing I can do with him."
The Master said: "People who spend the whole day together and never talk of what is right, who love to show off their small cleverness - they are hard to help."
The Master said: "The noble person takes what is right as his substance, practises it through ritual, speaks it with modesty, and brings it to completion with trustworthiness. That is a noble person."
The Master said: "A noble person is troubled by his own lack of ability, not by others' not knowing him."
The Master said: "A noble person dislikes the thought of passing away without his name being spoken of."
The Master said: "The noble person looks to himself; the petty person looks to others."
The Master said: "The noble person is dignified but does not quarrel, and is sociable but not partisan."
The Master said: "The noble person does not promote someone because of what he says, and does not dismiss what is said because of who says it."
Zigong asked: "Is there a single word that one can practise all one's life?" The Master said: "Is it not reciprocity? What you do not want for yourself, do not impose on others."
The Master said: "In my dealings with people, whom have I criticised, and whom have I praised? If I have praised anyone, it was because I had tested him. These are the people through whom the Three Dynasties followed the straight Way."
The Master said: "I can still remember when the historians left gaps in their records, and when someone who owned a horse lent it to others to ride. Now that is gone."
The Master said: "Clever words confuse virtue. Lack of patience in small matters confuses great plans."
The Master said: "When the multitude dislikes someone, you must look into it. When the multitude likes someone, you must look into it."
The Master said: "A person can enlarge the Way; the Way cannot enlarge a person."
The Master said: "To make a mistake and not correct it - that is what is called a mistake."
The Master said: "I once went a whole day without eating and a whole night without sleeping in order to think. It was no use. It is better to learn."
The Master said: "The noble person plans for the Way, not for food. In farming there is hunger; in learning there is salary. The noble person worries about the Way, not about poverty."
The Master said: "If one's wisdom reaches it but one's humaneness cannot hold it, then even if one gains it, one is sure to lose it. If one's wisdom reaches it and one's humaneness can hold it, but one does not govern with dignity, the people will not be respectful. If one's wisdom reaches it, one's humaneness can hold it, and one governs with dignity, but one does not move the people through ritual, it is still not good."
The Master said: "A noble person cannot be known through small matters, but can be given great responsibility. A petty person cannot be given great responsibility, but can be known through small matters."
The Master said: "People need humaneness more than they need water and fire. I have seen people die by stepping into water and fire; I have never seen anyone die by stepping into humaneness."
The Master said: "When it comes to humaneness, do not yield even to your teacher."
The Master said: "The noble person is firm in principle but does not hold to petty good faith."
The Master said: "In serving a ruler, put the work first and the salary after."
The Master said: "In teaching there should be no distinction of classes."
The Master said: "Those who follow different ways do not make plans together."
The Master said: "Language should simply communicate."
Music Master Mian came to see him. When he reached the steps, the Master said: "Here are the steps." When he reached the mat, the Master said: "Here is the mat." When all were seated, the Master told him: "So-and-so is here; so-and-so is here." When Music Master Mian had gone out, Zizhang asked: "Is that the way to speak with a music master?" The Master said: "Yes, that is certainly the way to help a music master."

keyLines.line: 君子固窮，小人窮斯濫矣
keyLines.en: The noble person bears poverty firmly; the petty person in poverty runs wild.
keyLines.note: The noble person keeps his integrity in want; the petty person in want will do anything.

keyLines.line: 予一以貫之
keyLines.en: I link it all together with one thread.
keyLines.note: Confucius said to Zigong: I am not a man of wide learning and strong memory, but I have one principle that runs through everything.

keyLines.line: 言忠信，行篤敬，雖蠻貊之邦行矣
keyLines.en: Speak loyally and truly, act sincerely and reverently, and you will get on even among the Man and Mo.
keyLines.note: If your words are faithful and true and your conduct earnest and reverent, you can get along even in the lands of the Man and Mo.

keyLines.line: 志士仁人，無求生以害仁，有殺身以成仁
keyLines.en: A man of purpose and a humane man do not seek life at the expense of humaneness; they would sooner lay down their lives to complete humaneness.
keyLines.note: Men of high aim and humane persons will not harm humaneness to save their lives; they will give up their lives to fulfil humaneness.

keyLines.line: 工欲善其事，必先利其器
keyLines.en: A craftsman who wishes to do his work well must first sharpen his tools.
keyLines.note: To do a good job one must first make one's tools sharp; a figure for needing good preparation first.

keyLines.line: 人無遠慮，必有近憂
keyLines.en: A man without far thought will have worry near at hand.
keyLines.note: If a person does not think far ahead, trouble will come close at hand.

keyLines.line: 躬自厚，而薄責於人，則遠怨矣
keyLines.en: Be strict with yourself and lenient in blaming others, and you will keep resentment at a distance.
keyLines.note: Blame yourself much and others little, and you will keep resentment away.

keyLines.line: 其恕乎！己所不欲，勿施於人
keyLines.en: Surely it is reciprocity! What you do not want yourself, do not do to others.
keyLines.note: Zigong asked if there is one word to practise for a lifetime. Confucius answered: perhaps 'reciprocity': what you do not want, do not do to others.

glossary.note: In this book, written 「陳」 for 「陣」: a battle formation. Confucius ran out of food on his way through the state of Chen.
The vessels of ancient sacrifice, standing for ritual.

glossary.en: wu wei er zhi - 'to rule by non-action'
glossary.note: Confucius praised Shun for ruling through virtue, without doing everything himself. It is not quite the same as Daoist non-action.
The wide belt tied at the waist by scholar-officials of old.
The popular music of the state of Zheng in the Spring and Autumn period, which Confucius thought too licentious.
The blind court musician of Lu, whose name was Mian.

pian15.background: In this book Confucius runs out of food in Chen and says the noble person bears poverty firmly, which is often quoted to encourage scholars to hold to the Way in hardship. 'What you do not want yourself, do not do to others' also appears in the book 'Yan Yuan'.

pian16.summary: Book 16, 'Ji shi', begins with the Ji family's attack on Zhuanyu and Confucius's criticism: do not worry about scarcity but about unequal shares; when the world has the Way, ritual, music and war come from the Son of Heaven. It then lists practical rules of self-cultivation: three beneficial friends, three joys, three cautions, three reverences and nine concerns.
pian16.translation:
The Ji family was about to attack Zhuanyu. Ran You and Jilu went to see Confucius and said: "The Ji family is about to take action against Zhuanyu." Confucius said: "Qiu! Is this not your fault? Zhuanyu was long ago appointed by the former kings to preside over the sacrifices on Mount Dongmeng, and it lies within the borders of our state; it is a minister of the altars of the land and grain. Why attack it?" Ran You said: "The Master's lord wants it. Neither of us two ministers wants it." Confucius said: "Qiu! Zhou Ren had a saying: 'Do your duty as far as your strength allows, and if you cannot, step down.' If a man in danger is not supported and if one who stumbles is not helped, what use is his assistant? And what you say is wrong. If a tiger or rhinoceros escapes from its cage, or a tortoise shell or jade is damaged in its box, whose fault is that?" Ran You said: "Now Zhuanyu is well fortified and close to Bi. If we do not take it now, it will become a worry to our descendants." Confucius said: "Qiu! A noble person despises those who avoid saying 'I want it' and are sure to make excuses for it. I have heard that those who hold a state or a family do not worry about having too little but about unequal shares; not about poverty but about unrest. If shares are equal there is no poverty; if there is harmony there is no scarcity; if there is peace there is no overthrow. This being so, if people from far away do not submit, cultivate culture and virtue to bring them. When they have come, make them content. Now You and Qiu assist your lord; far-off people do not submit and you cannot bring them; the state is breaking apart and you cannot hold it together; and you plan to use shields and spears within the state. I fear that the Ji family's troubles lie not in Zhuanyu but within their own screen wall."
Confucius said: "When the world has the Way, ritual, music and punitive expeditions come from the Son of Heaven. When the world lacks the Way, ritual, music and punitive expeditions come from the lords. When they come from the lords, it is rare for ten generations to pass without loss. When they come from the grandees, it is rare for five generations. When subordinate officials hold the fate of the state, it is rare for three generations. When the world has the Way, government is not in the hands of grandees. When the world has the Way, the common people do not criticise."
Confucius said: "The revenues left the ducal house five generations ago. Government passed to the grandees four generations ago. So the descendants of the Three Huan families are in decline."
Confucius said: "Three kinds of friends help you, and three kinds harm you. Friends who are upright, who are trustworthy, and who are well informed help you. Friends who are flatterers, who are smooth, and who are glib harm you."
Confucius said: "Three kinds of enjoyment help you, and three kinds harm you. To enjoy being guided by ritual and music, to enjoy speaking of others' good points, and to enjoy having many worthy friends help you. To enjoy extravagant pleasure, to enjoy idle wandering, and to enjoy feasting harm you."
Confucius said: "In attending a noble person there are three possible faults. To speak when it is not yet time to speak is called rashness. Not to speak when it is time to speak is called concealment. To speak without watching his expression is called blindness."
Confucius said: "A noble person guards against three things. In youth, when the blood and qi are not yet settled, he guards against lust. In the prime of life, when the blood and qi are at full strength, he guards against quarrelling. In old age, when the blood and qi have declined, he guards against greed."
Confucius said: "A noble person stands in awe of three things: the mandate of Heaven, great persons, and the words of the sages. The petty person does not know the mandate of Heaven and so does not fear it, is disrespectful to great persons, and mocks the words of the sages."
Confucius said: "Those born knowing are the highest. Those who know through learning are next. Those who learn after meeting difficulty are next again. Those who meet difficulty and do not learn are the lowest of the people."
Confucius said: "A noble person has nine concerns. In seeing, to see clearly. In hearing, to hear sharply. In expression, to be warm. In manner, to be respectful. In speech, to be loyal. In work, to be reverent. In doubt, to ask. In anger, to think of the consequences. In seeing a chance of gain, to think of what is right."
Confucius said: "'Seeing the good, act as if you could not catch up; seeing the bad, act as if testing boiling water.' I have seen such people and I have heard such words. 'Living in seclusion to pursue one's aims, practising what is right to carry out one's Way.' I have heard such words, but I have not seen such a person."
Duke Jing of Qi had a thousand teams of four horses, yet on the day he died the people could find no virtue in him to praise. Boyi and Shuqi starved at the foot of Mount Shouyang, and to this day the people praise them. Does this not mean the same?
Chen Kang asked Boyu: "Have you heard anything different from your father?" He replied: "No. Once he was standing alone and I was hurrying across the courtyard. He said, 'Have you studied the Songs?' I replied, 'Not yet.' 'If you do not study the Songs, you will have nothing to say.' I withdrew and studied the Songs. Another day, he was again standing alone and I was hurrying across the courtyard. He said, 'Have you studied ritual?' I replied, 'Not yet.' 'If you do not study ritual, you will have nowhere to stand.' I withdrew and studied ritual. I have heard these two things." Chen Kang withdrew, delighted, and said: "I asked one thing and got three: I heard about the Songs, I heard about ritual, and I heard that a noble person keeps his distance from his own son."
The wife of the ruler of a state: the ruler calls her 'Madam'; she calls herself 'Little Girl'; the people of the state call her 'Lord's Madam'; speaking to other states they call her 'Our Humble Little Lady'; people of other states also call her 'Lord's Madam'.

keyLines.line: 丘也，聞有國有家者，不患寡而患不均，不患貧而患不安
keyLines.en: I have heard that those who have a state or a family do not worry about scarcity but about unequal shares, not about poverty but about instability.
keyLines.note: Confucius said: those who rule a state or a house should worry not about few people but about unfair sharing, not about poverty but about unrest.

keyLines.line: 遠人不服，則修文德以來之
keyLines.en: If distant people do not submit, cultivate the civil virtues to draw them in.
keyLines.note: If people from afar do not come over, improve culture, teaching and virtuous government to attract them.

keyLines.line: 天下有道，則禮樂征伐自天子出；天下無道，則禮樂征伐自諸侯出
keyLines.en: When the world has the Way, ritual, music and punitive campaigns go out from the Son of Heaven; when the world lacks the Way, they go out from the feudal lords.
keyLines.note: When the world follows the Way, the Son of Heaven decides on ritual, music and war; when it does not, the lords do, then the grand masters, then their retainers, and the lower it goes the shorter it lasts.

keyLines.line: 友直，友諒，友多聞，益矣
keyLines.en: Friends who are upright, friends who are trustworthy, friends who are widely informed: these are beneficial.
keyLines.note: Three kinds of helpful friends: the upright, the trustworthy, and the well informed.

keyLines.line: 友便辟，友善柔，友便佞，損矣
keyLines.en: Friends who are smooth flatterers, friends who are soft and pliant, friends who are glib talkers: these are harmful.
keyLines.note: Three kinds of harmful friends: those used to fawning, those who flatter to your face and slander behind your back, and those with glib tongues.

keyLines.line: 少之時，血氣未定，戒之在色
keyLines.en: When young, while the blood and qi are not yet settled, guard against lust.
keyLines.note: The noble person has three cautions: in youth, against lust; in the prime of life, against quarrelling; in old age, against greed.

keyLines.line: 君子有三畏：畏天命，畏大人，畏聖人之言
keyLines.en: The noble person has three awes: he stands in awe of the mandate of Heaven, of great men, and of the words of the sages.
keyLines.note: The three things the noble person reveres: the mandate of Heaven, people of virtue and rank, and the words of the sages.

keyLines.line: 視思明，聽思聰，色思溫，貌思恭，言思忠，事思敬，疑思問，忿思難，見得思義
keyLines.en: In seeing, think of seeing clearly; in hearing, of hearing keenly; in expression, of being mild; in manner, of being respectful; in speech, of being loyal; in affairs, of being reverent; in doubt, of asking; in anger, of the consequences; in the sight of gain, of rightness.
keyLines.note: The noble person's nine concerns: to see clearly, to hear well, a mild face, a respectful manner, loyal words, careful action, asking when in doubt, thinking of trouble when angry, and thinking of rightness when seeing gain.

glossary.note: A small dependent state of Lu, in the region of today's Fei county in Shandong.
The screen inside the gate of a palace, a figure for trouble within.
The descendants of Duke Huan of Lu: the three families of Ji Sun, Shu Sun and Meng Sun.
People in the habit of fawning.
Kong Li, the son of Confucius; his courtesy name was Boyu.
A disciple of Confucius, courtesy name Ziqin.

pian16.background: This book lists the noble person's cultivation, friendships and awe in sets of three and nine. Its style differs a little from the other books and some scholars think it was compiled later, but its content is widely known.

pian17.summary: Book 17, 'Yang Huo', covers Confucius's remarks on taking office, study, filial piety, human nature, and ritual and music: 'by nature close together, by practice far apart', the six sayings and six blindnesses, the Songs that can rouse, observe, bring together and express grievance, 'does Heaven speak?', and the three years' mourning.
pian17.translation:
Yang Huo wanted to see Confucius, but Confucius would not see him, so he sent Confucius a gift of a roast piglet. Confucius waited until he was out and went to pay his respects, but they met on the road. Yang Huo said to Confucius: "Come, I want to talk with you. Can someone who keeps his treasure to himself while his state is in confusion be called humane?" "No." "Can someone who is eager to take part in affairs and yet keeps missing the chance be called wise?" "No." "The days and months are passing; the years do not wait for us." Confucius said: "Very well, I shall take office."
The Master said: "By nature people are close to one another; by practice they grow far apart."
The Master said: "Only the highest wisdom and the lowest folly do not change."
The Master went to Wucheng and heard the sound of string instruments and singing. He smiled and said: "Why use an ox-cleaver to kill a chicken?" Ziyou replied: "Some time ago I heard you say, Master: 'When a noble person studies the Way he loves people; when a petty person studies the Way he is easy to employ.'"
